#5912. The EU’s First AI Summit

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

World Brief: The EU’s First AI Summit

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the European Union’s artificial intelligence ambitions, dual car bombings in Russia, and an alleged Iranian strike on a U.S. radar system.

European Union leaders convened in Dublin on Friday for the bloc’s first-ever summit on artificial intelligence. With the continent expected to fall short of its chip-manufacturing goals, the conference may be a pivotal opportunity for the EU to develop a unified policy that aims to catch up with the world’s AI powerhouses: the United States and China.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the European Union’s artificial intelligence ambitions, dual car bombings in Russia, and an alleged Iranian strike on a U.S. radar system.

European Union leaders convened in Dublin on Friday for the bloc’s first-ever summit on artificial intelligence. With the continent expected to fall short of its chip-manufacturing goals, the conference may be a pivotal opportunity for the EU to develop a unified policy that aims to catch up with the world’s AI powerhouses: the United States and China.

The 2023 European Chips Act sought to double the continent’s semiconductor production global market share from roughly 10 percent to 20 percent by 2030 and attract billions of dollars in foreign tech investment. This legislation was a way for Europeans to say, “we want to be serious about this, and the only way to be competitive is to engage in the same practices, because otherwise you’re just never going to get manufacturing back to your shores,” Bruce Andrews, then-Intel’s corporate vice president, told FP’s Rishi Iyengar in 2024.

Since then, though, the EU has emerged as a more passive actor in AI’s advancement. A March report by Eurostat, the bloc’s statistics office, found that 1 in 5 EU enterprises used at least one AI technology in 2025, compared to less than 1 in 10 businesses a few years ago. Yet, in installed data center capacity alone, the bloc, with its 11.92 gigawatts, remains double-digits behind the United States (53.73 gigawatts) and China (31.9 gigawatts).

Such stagnation has EU leaders concerned that the continent is being left behind. “AI is the most important technology of our time,” European Council ‌President António Costa wrote on X on Friday. “Europe must make the most of its benefits, from higher productivity to better public services. We must also manage the risks and changes it will bring—and help set global standards for responsible governance and safe, human-centric AI.”

Yet the summit’s AI agenda may be derailed by other issues—particularly, who will represent European interests in future Russia-Ukraine peace talks.

On Thursday, Russian President Vladimir Putin told U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner that he would allow European officials to join the next round of negotiations. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who is also in Dublin this week for talks with EU leadership, applauded Putin’s concession. However, who will represent the continent’s delegation remains unclear.

“If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation,” Kushner said on Thursday. Among the names floated as possible options are Costa, EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is also likely to steal the summit’s attention. Huang stepped down on Thursday over his alleged extramarital affairs, including one that he admitted to with a suspected Chinese spy. Nvidia is the world’s leading producer of the advanced semiconductor chips used to power AI and data centers.

Assassination attempts. Russian authorities are investigating a series of assassination attempts this week, after two separate car bombings in as many days targeted senior pro-Kremlin officials. It is unclear who was responsible for the incidents; however, Ukraine’s intelligence agency has previously used similar operations to attack dozens of Russian officers and operatives. Kyiv has claimed responsibility for a few of these operations, including the killing of Lt. Gen. Igor Kirillov in December 2024, but it has not commented on this week’s bombings.

On Thursday, local media reported an explosion in St. Petersburg’s Pushkinsky District, an area known for housing Russian military personnel. The attack killed a senior Russian military official believed to be a colonel in the country’s air force. The following day, a car bomb in Moscow severely wounded Sergei Zavorotniy, a former senior aide to exiled former Ukrainian Prime Minister Mykola Azarov, who fled Kyiv in 2014 after Ukraine’s Maidan revolution toppled the country’s pro-Russian president.

Both attacks occurred following a new round of U.S.-mediated Russia-Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. Those negotiations made little headway, apart from an agreement to exchange prisoners. However, Putin later expressed his willingness to hold a future round of dialogue with European representatives present.

Alleged U.S.-Iran strikes. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed on Friday to have destroyed a U.S. early-warning radar system in Bahrain in what would be Tehran’s first direct attack on a U.S. military installation in months. The IRGC said the operation was in retaliation for a recent U.S. airstrike on an Iranian communications tower overlooking the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. Central Command, however, denied that its radar system was damaged, instead claiming to have intercepted two Iranian drones that were heading toward Bahrain.

The alleged radar system strike came the same day that a tanker carrying liquified natural gas (LNG) reportedly hit a naval mine in the strait. The IRGC navy told state media that the ship was using an “unauthorized and dangerous route” when it came into contact with the underwater explosive and that it had ignored repeated warnings to avoid the area.

As traffic through the critical passageway has started to return, the number of maritime incidents has also climbed. October was the busiest month for LNG exports from the Persian Gulf region since war first broke out in late February. According to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, though, last month also saw the highest number of attacks on ships in the strait.

Vance’s new mandate. U.S. President Donald Trump directed Vice President J.D. Vance to move off the Iran portfolio on Thursday and instead focus his “complete and total attention” on alleged corruption in Democratic Party-run states and cities. The shift comes after Vance blamed the administration’s handling of the Iran war for Democrats’ sweeping wins in recent midterm elections.

Vance has long had a heavy hand in U.S.-Iran negotiations. Despite being a skeptic of the war, the vice president has helped shape the conflict’s objectives, led the charge for a precarious memorandum of understanding, and engaged with top Iranian hard-liners to try to revive peace talks. Moving him off the Iran agenda therefore marks a significant shift in how Trump appears to want to handle the conflict.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

The change-up also signals the White House’s concerns about a looming Democrat-run Congress. Incoming Democratic lawmakers have vowed to investigate Trump’s business dealings and other potential avenues of corruption when they take power in January. In response on Thursday, Trump accused Democratic Party leadership—particularly in the states of California, Illinois, and Minnesota—of stealing billions of dollars every month, without citing evidence.

On Sunday, South African authorities announced the results from Nov. 4 local elections. Why was the election a historic one for the African National Congress party?

A. The party won a majority in every province except one. B. It marked the party’s worst-ever results. C. The party won a majority in the Western Cape province for the first time. D. Two-thirds of the party’s election winners were women.

Finland already has a reputation for being the happiest country in the world. Now, Helsinki is hoping to share that wealth with 16 lucky singles from around the world. In February, Finland will host a four-day, food-oriented group date alongside local Finnish residents also looking for love. Participants will taste some of the country’s most iconic dishes, from sautéed reindeer to bread cheese; relax in traditional saunas; and explore the Nordic nation’s cultural landmarks.

FP’s World Brief writer can personally attest that the Finnish sauna experience alone provides an almost unparalleled level of relaxation. Just follow the golden rule: What is said in the sauna stays in the sauna.

B. It marked the party’s worst-ever results.

No party won an outright majority, a further sign that South Africa’s political landscape is fragmenting, FP’s Nosmot Gbadamosi reports in Africa Brief.

#5911. What Republicans don’t know about Black voters’ resilience cost them

The campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads. The “pick another protein” spot will forever be stuck in the brains of a huge swath of Americans, especially Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. She underestimated Colom and his team, and will soon be an ex-senator.

However, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

The ad delivered an all-American lesson about history, born of bravery and sacrifice.

Filmed at the Jackson, Miss., home of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, the ad featured Colom recounting the story of Evers, a World War II veteran who survived Normandy, only to be shot in the back by a racist assassin, resentful that a Black man dared to exercise his rights as a citizen in the country he fought for.

“He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”

In a state where voting is still racially polarized, it was clear that Colom would not win over a majority of white voters; he won an estimated 25 percent, better than Democrats in recent elections and cutting into Trump’s margins, but certainly not a path to victory.

Black voters in Mississippi made the difference, as they often have. With their allies in the cause of justice, they heeded the call. They showed up despite the state’s stringent and often confusing voting restrictions, purges of the voting rolls engineered by Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson (who used unverified data from a credit bureau), and the U.S. Supreme Court Louisiana v. Callais decision that led to a wave of Southern states breaking up Black-majority districts.

When the Mississippi purges resulted in “affidavit ballots” that required verification to count, as The Washington Post reported, young Black women tracked down those voters, one by one, to do everything they could to ensure voters’ efforts were not in vain.

Black voters mattered in states all over the country, but especially in the South, where low turnout has plagued Democrats, particularly in midterm elections.

Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected the first Black female governor in the country in Georgia, where Democrats won up and down the ballot. Newly elected senators Annie Andrews in South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas campaigned for and earned support from Black voters with proposals that rose above platitudes. And don’t sleep on North Carolina, where voters flipped seats the GOP tried to gerrymander into a hardened majority. The sight of hundreds of students from HBCU NC A&T State University, denied a campus early voting site, marching to the polls, must have made the ancestors smile.

In Florida and Louisiana, where Democrats had little financial support and lost their statewide races, Black voters brought them tantalizingly close to victory and energized for the contests to come.

I still don’t expect Republicans to give up the election shenanigans, done in the name of “election integrity” and color blindness but in reality designed to demoralize as much as suppress. Why try to win over a diverse electorate with an inclusive, policy-driven message when manipulating Black-majority districts can still work?

The number of Black U.S. House members in the next session of Congress will fall, offset by a few Democrats who survived in redrawn districts, including Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina.

But you can’t redistrict a state, and you can’t skip town halls and expect tradition, support for the Confederacy and an “R” after your name to forever save you — the Hyde-Smith playbook.

"I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator," she bragged, too soon, on election night.

Maybe she should have emphasized affordability, saving rural hospitals and serving all Mississippians, as Colom did.

What did GOP officials in those Southern red states think they would accomplish by focusing on their base and ignoring everyone else in states they were supposed to be serving?

Did they not pay attention in history class, or maybe they attended one of those post-integration private schools where an unedited version of America’s past might not have been on the lesson plan?

Did they believe that voters who remembered Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer, Vernon Dahmer and countless others would shrug and say “you win” when legislatures and elections officials quickly and cynically pounced to quiet their voices?

That would be disrespectful to all the people who worked for, sometimes died for rights they knew they may never enjoy, yet had a belief in America and the rightness of their cause.

Scott Colom and the Evers family remembered. He was emotional in his reaction, in an MS NOW interview, when asked about the statement from Reena Evers-Everette, daughter of Medgar and Myrlie Evers. “Their courage helped make this moment possible,” she said.

Colum agreed: “I absolutely stand on their shoulders. And from the bottom of my heart, I’m going to do everything I can to make them proud.”

Post-election, he has been very gracious, saying that he intends to serve all Mississippians, including the woman whom I suspect would hit a different note if the election had turned in her favor.

I have no doubt Scott Colom means it. He knows who paid the price to get him this far.

#5910. Trump reversed the Pied Piper’s bargain, and voters stiffed him

When the pied piper loses his audience, we must ask whether the people have rediscovered their conscience or simply found a new tune to follow.

On Tuesday night, Donald Trump and his MAGA movement saw what happens when political influence collides with the everyday realities of the people it seeks to lead.

The 2026 midterm elections brought a dramatic shift in political power. Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, flipping Senate seats in states such as Texas and Kansas, which were long thought to be out of reach, and winning House districts Trump easily carried just two years ago.Â

Voter polls placed the presidentâs approval at approximately 38%, with roughly six in 10 voters saying he was a factor in their vote. But beneath those numbers lies a more consequential story. Americans are confronting the cost of living, the economic consequences of tariffs, the uncertainty of war with Iran and diminishing confidence in American leadership abroad.

Trump promised his voters he would drain the swamp, end foreign wars and bring prices down. Yet many Americans went to the polls questioning whether those promises had been kept. Unlike the Pied Piper of Hamelin, who rid the town of its rats, Trump now faces an electorate concerned that the problems he promised to eliminate have instead multiplied.Â

In the original story, the Piper fulfilled his bargain. He played his pipe, led the rats into the river and freed the town. But when the townspeople refused to pay him, he returned to exact revenge by leading away their children.Â

Over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.

Critics argue that Trump reversed that bargain. Rather than delivering the relief promised to ordinary Americans, the administration has left many struggling with economic uncertainty while continuing to demand political loyalty. Over and over again throughout the midterm campaign, Trump urged supporters to vote as though he were personally on the ballot. In this telling, the Piper did not eliminate the rats. He added to them, and still he expected to be paid.Â Â

Trumpâs supporters see a different story. They point to immigration raids and mass deportations, deregulation and challenges to established political institutions as evidence that the president delivered on important commitments. From their perspective, voters who rejected those policies after experiencing the consequences resemble townspeople who accepted the Piperâs services, but refused to honor their bargain.Â

Both interpretations expose a fundamental ethical question: When does political loyalty cease to be an expression of shared principles and become an abdication of independent judgment?Â

In a democracy, voters are not obligated to follow the music indefinitely. They retain the right to question the destination, reconsider promises and withdraw their support. Political loyalty is not a debt citizens owe their leaders. It is a trust that leaders must continually earn.

Albert Hirschman, an American economist and author of âExit, Voice, and Loyalty: Responses to Decline in Firms, Organizations, and States,â distinguished between voice (working to change an organization from within) and exit (abandoning it). A vote against an incumbent is often itself an act of a voice. But where voters withdrew their allegiance from a party or movement altogether, Tuesday looked more like an exit. Hirschman saw loyalty as what keeps members inside, speaking up rather than leaving. His framework suggests that when loyalty silences voice instead, exit becomes the only remaining option.Â

But elected officials carry a different and greater responsibility.Â

Like the children of Hamelin, many Republican lawmakers followed the music toward an uncertain destination. Unlike those children, however, they had the authority â and the responsibility â to question where they were being led. Some embraced the presidentâs direction; others followed him despite reservations, knowing that dissent could invite a primary challenge. After all, they had seen others who challenged his leadership pay a considerable political cost. Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie and Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy lost their Republican primaries to Trump-backed challengers.Â

Political cooperation is essential to governing. But cooperation becomes ethically troubling when loyalty to an individual displaces the obligation to question, deliberate and act independently. The oath of office is not a pledge of allegiance to a president, a party or a political movement. It is a commitment to uphold the Constitution. A president can command attention, share public debate and place enormous pressure on members of his own party. But the ability to demand loyalty does not create a moral entitlement to receive it.Â

The children of Hamelinâs Pied Piper tale had no part in the broken bargain, yet they paid its price. In our democracy, ordinary Americans and future generations often inherit the consequences of political decisions, and today they are paying a price. Economic instability, weakened public trust and the costs of war do not disappear when an election ends. A leaderâs success cannot be measured solely by the number of people willing to follow along with them. It must also be measured by what happens to those who never chase the tune.Â

The election has shifted power in Washington. Democrats, after winning sizable, historic victories throughout the country, will soon have an opportunity to exercise congressional oversight and reinforce the institutional independence our constitutional system requires.Â

But changing who holds the instrument does not necessarily change the music.Â

Democrats now face their own ethical test. Will they exercise power with the transparency, accountability and respect for constitutional checks they demanded from their opponents? Will they welcome dissent within their own ranks? And will they resist the temptation to substitute partisan loyalty for independent judgment?Â Â

An election can change the balance of power overnight. It cannot, by itself, restore public trust or guarantee ethical leadership. That requires leaders willing to place constitutional responsibility above political convenience, institutions prepared to exercise meaningful oversight, and citizens who refuse to surrender their judgment to the most compelling voice in the room. The first six months of the 120th Congress must be defined not merely by a change in political power, but by a demonstrable commitment to ethical reform, transparency, and accountability. The American people did not vote simply for a change in leadership. They voted for a government worthy of their trust.

The Pied Piperâs greatest power was not simply his ability to play a captivating tune. It was his ability to persuade others to follow without questioning where their journey would end.Â

Political ethicist Dennis Thompson called this the problem of many hands: When many officials each contribute a small part to a collective outcome, responsibility seems to dissolve until no one bears it. So, when political loyalty becomes more important than independent judgment, who bears responsibility â the leader who plays the tune, or those who willingly follow? Thompsonâs framework does not allow individual lawmakers to hide behind presidential leadership, party discipline or collective decisions. Nor does it assign blame equally. Responsibility depends on each officialâs authority, knowledge, contribution and the alternatives available to them. By that measure, those who knew better and had the power to act cannot claim they were merely following the music from the leader in the red hat.

When the music finally stops, the question is not simply who will lead next.Â

It is whether we have learned to listen differently.

#5908. Lessons From the Watergate Babies for the ‘No Kings’ Congress

Analysis: Lessons From the Watergate Babies for the ‘No Kings’ Congress

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Democrats scored a stunning victory in the 2026 midterms. Although many pollsters predicted a strong showing for the party out of power, few expected the map to look so blue by the end. In some ways, Texas looked as Democratic as New York or California.

Now the question for Democrats is: What comes next?

Democrats scored a stunning victory in the 2026 midterms. Although many pollsters predicted a strong showing for the party out of power, few expected the map to look so blue by the end. In some ways, Texas looked as Democratic as New York or California.

Now the question for Democrats is: What comes next?

However large their majorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate, they will face a Republican president who is extraordinarily aggressive in his use of executive power, as well as a Supreme Court that has been generally sympathetic to his vision of the presidency. If Democrats pass legislation, President Donald Trump will likely veto it. If Democrats investigate him, he will stonewall and wield his pardon power for allies who do the same. If they try to stop the war in Iran, he will draw on decades of accumulated presidential war powers to keep doing what he wants.

But the 120th Congress is not the first to face such a difficult situation. In 1975, the new class of House and Senate Democrats elected in the aftermath of President Richard Nixon’s resignation squared off against Republican President Gerald Ford. For all his talk of healing the nation and moving beyond the most contentious issues of the moment, Ford was also willing to use the veto to cut the Democratic Congress down to size. Though he understood that in Nixon’s shadow he had to scale back the presidency, he was not willing to give up the many tools at his disposal.

Yet the 94th Congress—propelled by the Watergate Babies, as they were known—found ways to use its legislative power to pursue internal reform, advance a legislative agenda, and help create the conditions for Jimmy Carter’s election in 1976. Democratic members of the incoming “No Kings Congress,” as we might call it, should take notes.

In November 1974, the nation was reeling from division, scandal, and crisis. A decade of domestic conflict over race relations and the Vietnam War had opened deep rifts throughout U.S. society. Public trust in government had plummeted, largely as a result of the war. The economy was also in shambles in the early part of the decade, as the United States, which had enjoyed unprecedented economic growth after World War II, suffered from unemployment, inflation, and an oil embargo.

Then came Watergate. Richard Nixon revealed what an imperial presidency looked like. Not only did he continue with secret military operations in Southeast Asia despite having promised to end the war in Vietnam, but he used the executive branch to intimidate, spy on, and threaten U.S. citizens; impounded money that Congress had appropriated; and engaged in dirty tricks against his opponents. As the scandal unfolded between 1972 and 1974, a story that began with a break-in at the Democratic National Committee Headquarters in the Watergate Complex grew into something much bigger: a revelation about the abuse of power that culminated in Nixon’s resignation, after being told that many Senate Republicans would vote to remove him from office if the House of Representatives passed articles of impeachment. After Nixon left office, Ford eroded the goodwill the public had for him by pardoning Nixon for any crimes that he might have committed. Ford’s approval ratings plummeted and many Americans came to see him as part of the problem.

The midterm campaigns had centered on the economy and on corruption in the political system. Democratic candidates promised a robust response to Americans’ pocketbook struggles and vowed to fix the problems the scandal had exposed in the political system. The midterms delivered a body blow to Republicans, even though they still controlled the White House. Democrats gained 49 seats in the House, bringing their total to 291, and a net of four seats in the Senate.

A new generation of House Democrats—such as Henry Waxman and George Miller (California), Tom Harkin (Iowa), Chris Dodd (Connecticut), Tim Wirth (Colorado), Thomas Downey (New York), and Paul Simon (Illinois)—came to Capitol Hill not wedded to older axioms and determined to bring about change. The day after voting, James Naughton of the New York Times wrote, “Democrats swept yesterday toward domination of the next Congress as voters across the nation apparently blamed Republicans for the Watergate scandal and for economic disruption.”

Looking back at the period, two of the Watergate Babies, Downey and Toby Moffett of Connecticut, recalled in a recent column in the Hartford Courant: “We were determined to challenge a sclerotic Congress where entrenched power sapped the idealism and creativity of newcomers. Led by the activism of new members — and supported by a key group of existing policymakers, dozens of newly empowered subcommittee chairs launched investigations on clean air violations, nuclear plant safety, pharmaceutical pricing and human rights abuses abroad — we had idealism, the staff, and the authority to change the way Congress functioned.”

But in November 1974, just as in November 2026, it was not clear what this new Congress would be able to accomplish. The government was divided, Democrats themselves were still split between a liberal northern and a conservative southern wing, and public distrust was so high that voters would be difficult to satisfy regardless of who was in power.

Yet the Democrats found a way to keep moving forward. Their first step was to clean up their own institution before turning on to the presidency. In December 1974, Democrats pressured Arkansan Wilbur Mills, the powerful chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, to step aside as a result of a scandal that involved his relationship with a local stripper named Fanne Foxe and his addiction to pills and alcohol. In January 1975, the freshman class of Watergate Babies led the drive to depose three other House committee chairmen—F. Edward Hébert, W.R. Poage, and Wright Patman—after questioning every sitting chairman about how responsive he would be to the party caucus and finding them wanting. The spirit of reform also reached the Senate, where Democrats tweaked the committee system and also lowered the number of votes needed to end a filibuster from two-thirds of the senators present and voting to three-fifths of senators.

Congress also investigated the Ford administration. In October 1974, Ford appeared before the House Judiciary Committee to answer tough questions about pardoning Nixon. New York Rep. Otis Pike and Idaho Sen. Frank Church led high-level hearings investigating the Cold War national security state, producing bombshell revelations about how officials had abused their authority and lied to the public, building public support for reforms that ultimately passed in 1978.

The 94th Congress also legislated. On some issues, it found points of agreement with Ford, who signed legislation providing tax rebates, creating the Earned Income Tax Credit, and establishing the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and CAFE fuel economy standards. In some cases, such as a bill funding public works jobs, Democrats overrode the president’s veto after scaling back the measure. In others, such as farm price supports, they passed bills that Ford successfully vetoed but that showed what the party might do in power. They had the effect of pushing voters to think about “what if?”—what if Democrats also had control of the White House? Some of the new Democrats, like Waxman, used their media platforms to promote issues, such as clean air legislation, that were only starting to gain attention.

In 1976, former Georgia Gov. Jimmy Carter won the presidency with 297 electoral votes. Although Carter was not a Washington insider, his campaign built on many of the themes that the 94th Congress had advanced and kept the same agenda: government reform, transparency, help for working Americans, and restoring the balance of power in Washington. Democrats also maintained massive majorities, with 292 seats in the House and 61 in the Senate.

The lesson from the Democrats of the 94th is that Congress can still accomplish a great deal in 2027, whether Trump chooses to govern in a transactional fashion with Democratic leadership or whether he decides to double down and fight.

Given the election results, Democrats can investigate corruption, conflicts of interest, and decision-making on matters such as Iran. Congress can work on cleaning up its own house, including legislation to restrict stock trading by sitting members. As Moffett and Downey wrote in the Hartford Courant, congressional reform is even more essential than in 1975, due to the erosion of staffing, expertise, and institutional knowledge. They propose revitalizing subcommittees as a first major step toward the path of reconstruction.

The No Kings Congress can look for legislation on pressing problems such as healthcare costs or Social Security that a lame duck president sees as being in his interest to reform, or that a shattered congressional Republican Party perceives as being in its own interest to join with the opposition on (thus making a bill veto proof). And Congress can keep pushing legislation on issues such as affordability and immigration that lets voters see what unified Democratic control might accomplish in 2029.

The one thing the 120th Congress can’t afford to do is nothing. A massive electorate and a diverse caucus, ranging from progressives in Michigan to preachers in Kansas, put Democrats into power. Voters have sent many signals that they want their leaders to do something about the crushing burden of affordability that weighs on U.S. families, the corruption that has afflicted Washington, and the sense of runaway presidential power. If Democrats live up to the moment, they could find themselves, two years from now, in an even stronger position to bring the era of MAGA to a decisive end.

Julian E. Zelizer is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a professor of history and public affairs at Princeton University. He is the author of The Long View, a newsletter putting the news in perspective. #5906. Some records in Ilhan Omar case will be released, judge says

A judge said he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

Judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

“This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg said.

The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

Boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he said next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”

The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

“You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg said.

Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump said last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

Separately, Boasberg said he may issue rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

For years Trump has said he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

#5905. Gay candidates won where it was supposed to be impossible

On Tuesday night, two things happened at once, and the country will be tempted to remember only one of them.

The first made me go quiet at my kitchen table. Chris Pappas won election to the U.S. Senate in New Hampshire, becoming the first openly gay man ever sent to that chamber, and part of the margin that handed Democrats the Senate. In Indiana, J.D. Ford, the first openly gay person ever elected to that stateâs legislature, unseated a Republican incumbent and is headed to the House. In Texas, of all places, James Talarico beat Ken Paxton to become the first Democrat to win statewide in more than thirty years, after a campaign in which anti-LGBTQ+ messaging was reportedly Paxtonâs single largest category of advertising, and in which the vice president of the United States stood on a stage and used âgayâ as a punchline against him. Talarico is straight, and he won anyway.

And on Long Island, in a district Donald Trump carried, a gay Democrat named Chris Gallant, whose private photographs were leaked against him precisely because someone believed that seeing him would be enough to end him, came within about two points of flipping a seat the forecasters had rated safely Republican. He conceded the election on Wednesday, down by roughly 6,700 votes in the closest race of the incumbent Republican Nick LaLotaâs career. In the same breath, Gallant called LaLota a brother in arms and told the district he was still their neighbor, which is to say he refused the shame he was supposed to feel from the photo leak to the very end. Whatever that is, it is not the story of a man sunk by leather. It is the story of a man who nearly won the unwinnable while carrying the exact weight that was supposed to be disqualifying.

In 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip.

Put those results next to one another and a sentence forms that would have been unimaginable a decade ago: In 2026, you cannot reliably win an American election by making a manâs gayness, real or invented, the center of your campaign. Republicans tried it in Texas and lost the whole state. They tried it on Long Island and watched a red seat nearly flip. The oldest weapon in the drawer â the one that raised me, the one that could empty a lunch table in the 1990s â is losing its edge at the ballot box. Voters keep looking at the openly gay candidate and sending him to Washington.

That is the headline, and it is real, and I am not going to let anyone talk me out of being moved by it.

But here is the second thing that happened Tuesday night. In the same hours, often on the same ballots, and it is the part the rainbow-wave coverage is already rushing past. In Arizona and Nebraska, voters approved measures to bar transgender girls from girlsâ sports. In Colorado, two measures aimed at transgender young people, one on sports and one restricting certain surgical care for minors, are narrowly passing. In Washington State, an initiative to keep transgender girls out of girlsâ sports passed comfortably. The same electorate that refused to punish a Senate candidate for being gay reached down the ballot and punished trans kids for existing.

This is the thing I need people to see before the celebration hardens into a story we tell ourselves. The contempt did not disappear on Tuesday. It relocated. A political movement that has learned it can no longer win by hating gay men has not given up the strategy. It has updated the target. The MAGA machine that aired the Paxton ads and laughed at Vanceâs joke is the same one now writing ballot measures about 11-year-olds, because cruelty still tests well when it is aimed at the group with the least power to answer back. Gays are simply the part of the community that got powerful enough to be left alone.

I know this pattern in my body, because I have watched it my whole life. The fear moves. First it was the plague, then it was the gay man as predator, then it was marriage as the end of the world, and each time the broader culture eventually got bored or ashamed and the fear went looking for a new address. Right now the address is a trans child in a locker room. The people who found that child did not arrive by accident. They are the same people, running the same play, because it is the only play they have ever had.

So I want to be careful about the victory lap, even as I take one. It is a genuine and hard-won thing that Chris Pappas will be a senator and J.D. Ford will be a congressman, and that a straight man in Texas could not be destroyed by being called gay. Those wins are not small, and the people who did the work to make them real earned every bit of the joy.Â

But a movement does not get to accept its own seats at the table while the youngest and most defenseless members of its own community are voted off the field in four states on the same night. This is not a win we get to keep cleanly. It is a split screen, and if we only look at our half of it, we become exactly the kind of people who could be bought off with a little representation while someone else pays the bill.

The refusal to be ashamed won some rooms on Tuesday. I felt it. The task now is to extend that refusal to the people the machine has decided to hunt next, to say as loudly for trans kids what the voters of New Hampshire and Indiana and Texas just said for us: that you do not get to make a personâs existence a punchline, or a wedge, or a ballot measure. We learned that lesson about gay men the slow and brutal way. The whole point of learning it is to spare the next group from learning it alone.

Chris Gallant did not quite win. But he came close enough to prove the old weapon is dulling. The question Tuesday really asked is whether we will hand the people wielding it a new one, or finally take the thing out of their hands.

Two years ago, Linda-Gail Bekker was jubilant. She had just led a major clinical trial in South Africa, the epicenter of the global HIV epidemic, testing a new form of prevention that was astonishingly effective. The drug, lenacapavir, is a pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which blocks the virus from spreading in HIV-negative people. A twice-yearly injection could replace daily pills, offering longer-lasting protection and thus slowing the spread of the virus.

When Bekker, the CEO of the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation in Cape Town, South Africa, announced the results of her trial at the International AIDS Conference in Munich in July 2024, the room erupted in a standing ovation. “There was huge anticipation and excitement. And then January came around, and suddenly that all disappeared,” she said, referring to the start of U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term.

The drug, lenacapavir, is a pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which blocks the virus from spreading in HIV-negative people. A twice-yearly injection could replace daily pills, offering longer-lasting protection and thus slowing the spread of the virus.

When Bekker, the CEO of the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation in Cape Town, South Africa, announced the results of her trial at the International AIDS Conference in Munich in July 2024, the room erupted in a standing ovation. “There was huge anticipation and excitement. And then January came around, and suddenly that all disappeared,” she said, referring to the start of U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term.

The Trump administration took a chainsaw to global health programs, including the U.S. President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), which has provided around $8 billion to South Africa since 2003. South Africa pays for most of its own HIV programs, including 90 percent of its antiretroviral drugs. Still, the collapse of PEPFAR was devastating, shuttering clinics for high-risk groups and leaving thousands of health workers without jobs.

South Africa is home to around 8 million people living with HIV, or around 20 percent of the global HIV population. Approximately 6 million of them are on treatment, but the country still records around 170,000 new infections each year.

When South Africa began rolling out lenacapavir this summer, the landscape had changed dramatically. U.S.-South Africa relations have deteriorated, as Trump has objected to South Africa’s genocide case against Israel in the International Court of Justice and accused the country of committing genocide against white Afrikaners. Those tensions have compounded uncertainty for the HIV program.

Last year, the United States provided South Africa with $115 million to keep core HIV services running, but in June, the Trump administration said it would end all PEPFAR funding for the country in the coming months. Washington also excluded South Africa from global health financing deals struck this year with other African countries. Even as the United States supports the lenacapavir launch elsewhere, it isn’t doing so in South Africa.

In an email, a U.S. State Department spokesperson confirmed that the political rift played a role in the decision to phase out PEPFAR funding. The spokesperson said PEPFAR was never meant to be a permanent initiative and that South Africa is “more than capable of supporting its own health programs” as a middle-income country.

It’s a departure from decades of U.S. foreign policy, said Jirair Ratevosian, a former senior PEPFAR official under President Joe Biden. “South Africa and the United States have never been perfectly aligned on foreign policy,” Ratevosian said. But the United States “was able to compartmentalize those disagreements and still cooperate on other big areas of interest that were aligned, and HIV was always one of those.”

Now, South Africa is left to manage its lenacapavir rollout without its historically biggest donor. It’s an early test of whether the country’s post-PEPFAR transition can become a blueprint for weathering the U.S. retreat from global health—or is a cautionary tale.

South African officials have downplayed the loss of U.S. support. In June, a health ministry spokesperson urged people not to panic, saying the government has “long been working on a self-reliance plan.” Officials have not released a formal plan, but they point to local drug manufacturing, stronger public health systems, and regional collaboration on HIV as important steps.

South Africa had a head start in this effort, as PEPFAR already accounted for less than 25 percent of the country’s HIV prevention funding, compared with around 80 percent in neighboring Mozambique and Zimbabwe, according to the Joint U.N. Program on HIV/AIDS last year.

At the launch of the lenacapavir rollout in June, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told a stadium crowd that the drug would mark a “turning point” for South Africa. Prevention remains a challenge in the country; until now PrEP has only been widely available as a daily pill, which can be difficult to access or stay on. South Africa planned to roll out a different shot that offers two months of protection last year, but high prices and PEPFAR disruptions stalled that effort.

Experts think the twice-yearly lenacapavir shot could be a game-changer. Modeling suggests that if between 1.7 million and 2.9 million South Africans get on lenacapavir each year, new infections could fall by as much as 31 percent, potentially allowing the country to eliminate HIV as a public health threat as soon as 2039. But first, South Africa must get the drug to people who need it.

In June, Ramaphosa said 3 million people will be offered lenacapavir over the next three years. The government has already secured enough doses to cover 456,000 people, funded with $29.2 million from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria. The first tranche was allocated to 360 public health facilities in high-burden districts, but as of mid-October, just under 79,000 South Africans had started lenacapavir, according to health ministry data.

Activists are frustrated by what they view as a sluggish rollout driven by funding gaps, insufficient planning, and regulatory bottlenecks. Some South African clinics have turned away patients seeking lenacapavir, some after running out of doses and others over logistical problems. Early in the rollout, facilities in the capital of Pretoria lacked HIV testing kits—a prerequisite to get the shot—or had not yet trained nurses to administer the drug.

“It’s a drip feed of supplies,” said Fatima Hassan, a human rights lawyer and the founder of the Health Justice Initiative in Cape Town. The U.S. funding cuts and the pace of the rollout are “putting our entire health system in jeopardy and all the gains we’ve made in the last 20 years at risk.”

The government has tried to plug some of the funding gaps left by the United States. Last year, the South African Treasury allocated around $45 million in emergency funding to cover some HIV programs, roughly one-tenth of what PEPFAR contributed in 2024. But that money does not resolve the question of what will happen to these services in the long term.

The State Department spokesperson said the United States would “reconsider future health assistance during the phase-out period”—but only if South Africa takes “concrete, demonstrable action” to remedy the Trump administration’s accusations that its government seizes land from white farmers, among other complaints.

South African Health Minister Aaron Motsoaledi has said the country plans to eventually finance its lenacapavir program itself, with help from donors. “To establish a couple million doses-deep lenacapavir program in the next couple of years, we will need outside help,” said Gesine Meyer-Rath, a health economist at the University of the Witwatersrand and Boston University.

But it is not yet clear which donors will provide that help. The Global Fund, which supported the initial rollout, plans to cut South Africa’s HIV/AIDS funding by 26 percent in its next allocation cycle as it tightens its focus on the poorest countries hit hardest by HIV, TB, and malaria. A South African health ministry spokesperson did not respond to questions about the lenacapavir rollout or its “self-reliance plan.”

South Africa is betting that a generic form of lenacapavir will hit the market just as the initial supply runs out, allowing the government to roll out the drug to hundreds more clinics. Gilead Sciences, the U.S. developer of lenacapavir, agreed to make a generic version available in 120 lower- and middle-income countries, including South Africa, for $40 per person per year; it is expected by the end of the year in Zambia and elsewhere in 2027. The Global Fund negotiated a confidential price with the drugmaker for the initial shots in South Africa and other recipient countries, but brand-name lenacapavir goes for roughly $28,000 per person per year in the United States. South African health officials say the generic price must be brought down to $25 to guarantee “universal access.”

Eventually, South Africa wants to manufacture lenacapavir itself, but that effort has also encountered roadblocks. In 2024, three South African pharmaceutical companies asked Gilead for permission to make generic versions, but they were rejected because they could not handle the 28-step process of synthesizing the drug’s active ingredient. South Africa’s government is now working with Gilead and technical advisors to make local production possible.

Clinicians and civil society groups warn that supply isn’t the only problem—it’s also about getting the lenacapavir shots to those who need it most, including sex workers, men who have sex with men, transgender people, and injectable drug users. But the 12 PEPFAR-funded specialized clinics and community-based outreach for these key populations, which served more than 63,000 people, have not been replaced.

“I do not think that the people who are suffering access issues because of the PEPFAR cuts are going to be the ones to get the drug,” said Kate Rees, a public health specialist at the Anova Health Institute, which suspended its PEPFAR-funded programs. “We know how to reach key populations, and waiting for them in the clinic is not it.”

Meyer-Rath, the health economist, said she has attended early planning meetings with government officials who want to reopen services for these populations and try to integrate patients into public health facilities—but that the budget available is “nonexistent or marginal.”

Another challenge: PEPFAR covered around 40 percent of South Africa’s HIV data workforce, which tracks infections and treatment uptake in HIV hot spots. With fewer of those workers, the patients who miss out on lenacapavir because they fall through the cracks of the traditional health system—as vulnerable groups tend to do—may go uncounted, making it harder to identify problems and surge support where it’s needed.

The next phase of the lenacapavir rollout is fast approaching, and it will test the country’s infrastructure as well as its supply. The first South Africans to receive the drug are due for their second shot in December, and clinics must provide an HIV test and an injection for each of them every six months going forward.

South Africa’s experience is likely to shape rollouts elsewhere, but other early adopters offer their own lessons. Kenya, which launched the drug in February, has used drop-in centers to reach key populations, though it has also struggled with shortages. Meanwhile, Zambia launched with just 500 doses in late 2025, and up to 85 percent of patients there and in Eswatini—which shares a border with South Africa—have returned on time for their second shot, according to Bhekisisa, a South African media outlet.

Lenacapavir is now being scaled up in 12 low- and middle-income countries, with 17 more countries due to receive it by early 2027, according to AVAC, an HIV prevention advocacy group. The rollout of generic lenacapavir next year will be another turning point. It’s a reminder that even if South Africa sticks the landing, there’s still a long way to go to defeat HIV.

“Right now, we are wobbling a bit, and the world is watching us wobble,” Meyer-Rath said. “But basically, it’s either the [South African] government or it’s not. No one will fund the system. We have to.”

Gabriela Galvin is an award-winning freelance journalist in London. She covers health and social policy.

#5902. These incoming members of Congress have been here before

When Rep.-elect Chris Rabb first worked on Capitol Hill in the 1990s, it didn’t exactly inspire him to want to go into politics.

“I said, ‘Oh, this is how the sausage is made? I should be a vegan,’” the Pennsylvania Democrat recalled.

Working for Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman elected as a U.S. senator, Rabb saw threats and “just vile things” directed at her.

“My entrée to service behind the scenes was seeing voluminous amounts of violence, hate speech and death threats against my boss, and I thought to myself, ‘Why would anyone want to serve?’” he said.

During his time in the state legislature starting in 2017, Rabb “fell in love with public service, despite the vitriol.” Now, the democratic socialist describes coming to Congress as “surreal,” as he succeeds retiring Rep. Dwight Evans in a deep-blue district based in West Philadelphia.

Rabb is one of more than a dozen incoming members who have worked on the Hill before, ranging from interns to chiefs of staff and everything in between.

Unlike some in the 100-plus-strong freshman class, they already know their way around the hallways. And Rabb has some advice for his new colleagues: “Treat your staff well. Take care of your staff; they’ll take care of you.”

Here are some of the former staffers who will join the House in January.

A couple years ago, Killin was working as chief of staff to former second gentleman Doug Emhoff. But she started out on the Hill.

“It is helpful to know, as I joke, where the bathrooms are, but I still feel like I have a lot to learn,” said the Army veteran, who unseated Republican Rep. Jeff Crank in a Colorado Springs-area district.

She served as the top staffer for three House Democrats: Donna Shalala of Florida, Carolyn Maloney of New York and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington.

“I’ve actually opened up two freshman offices, so it’s helpful to have done that before,” Killin said.

White will be just the third person in modern times to hold the job of nonvoting D.C. delegate. He replaces retiring Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton — also his former boss.

Before his time on the D.C. Council, he worked as her legislative counsel, watching her navigate a role with limited power in her perennial fight for statehood.

“I need to make sure I’m developing a national profile for this seat,” he said, vowing to continue the quest for full representation even as President Donald Trump seeks to exert more control over the District.

One of just a few Republican women in the freshman class, Gruters said she “never in a million years” imagined coming to Congress herself, despite her years as a staffer.

She will replace retiring Rep. Vern Buchanan in Florida’s 16th District, after once serving as his operations director. She also worked as district director for Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla.

“I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Gruters, whose husband leads the Republican National Committee.

Rogers added another title to his résumé last week: freshman class president.

His fellow incoming Republicans tapped him for the role. Not so long ago, he was working for the Senate Judiciary Committee, fresh off a stint at the white-shoe law firm White & Case.

In 2025 he served as general counsel for Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., and plans to keep pushing for a bill he helped draft that aims to crack down on foreign surrogacy contracts. “We are currently selling American children to China, our No. 1 adversary,” Rogers said, describing it as “deplorable.”

Rogers will succeed retiring GOP Rep. Neal Dunn in the Florida Panhandle.

García’s run for her boss’s seat drew controversy from the start. When Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García, D-Ill., waited to publicly announce his retirement until after the filing deadline in Illinois had already passed, critics blasted him for effectively boxing out other candidates and clearing the way for his chief of staff.

He faced a rare formal disapproval vote in the House over the move. But García has insisted she is more than a hand-picked successor, saying on her campaign website that she has “delivered solutions rooted in lived experience.”

The son of Ghanaian immigrants, Boafo is a state delegate who has lobbied on the Hill for tech company Oracle.

He also worked as campaign manager for Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, earning an endorsement from the retiring longtime Democrat and campaign cash from groups aligned with him.

Boafo prevailed in a crowded primary, even as Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi threw her weight behind a different candidate, former Capitol Police officer Harry Dunn.

Sell worked under then-House Agriculture Chair Larry Combest during the 2000 crop insurance overhaul and the fight over the 2002 farm bill. He later joined his former boss in launching an agricultural lobbying firm, Combest, Sell and Associates.

Once a precocious child magician who wrote his own book of tricks, Lasher also got an early start in politics.

“I feel supremely fortunate to have wandered into Jerry Nadler’s political orbit as a teenager 30 years ago, and then to have worked in his congressional office a decade later,” Lasher wrote in an opinion piece for City & State New York.

Backed by the retiring Nadler, the self-described “nerd” beat out a couple of big names in the primary, including a Kennedy family heir. Another former boss endorsed him, too: Gov. Kathy Hochul. Before serving as a New York state assemblyman, Lasher worked as her policy director.

Villegas ousted GOP Rep. David Valadao in a closely watched race in the San Joaquin Valley.

A decade ago, he was an intern for Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif. And in a twist, the progressive also interned for one of his primary opponents, former California state Rep. Rudy Salas.

A San Diego City councilmember, Von Wilpert flipped the seat held by Republican Rep. Darrell Issa, who decided not to run for reelection under a map redrawn by Democrats.

When she worked for the National Labor Relations Board in 2016, she was detailed to the House Education and Labor Committee, working under ranking member Robert C. Scott, D-Va.

Jackie Wang and Nick Eskow contributed to this report.

#5901. Goodbye from Salon

Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.

Itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.

When Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.

Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.

The history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.

The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.

Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.

Thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.

#5900. Democrats Can’t Return to Pre-Trump Foreign Policy

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Argument: Democrats Can’t Return to Pre-Trump Foreign Policy

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

With Democrats in decisive control of the 120th Congress, the time has come for the party to offer a vision for what comes next for U.S. foreign policy. The country’s stunning repudiation of U.S. President Donald Trump is stoking the temptation to embrace a sharp policy reversal, on the assumption that the center of American democracy has held and the pre-Trump foreign-policy consensus can, too. However, when it comes to working with U.S. allies, that would be a grave mistake.

The next Congress has an important role to play in defining this new foreign-policy vision—one that the next president could build upon in 2029. In asserting its powers to conduct oversight, legislate, and conduct its own diplomacy, the Democratic majority should be seeking to put in place elements of a new U.S. approach, rather than simply reverse the Trumpian damage. Doing so will begin to reorient U.S. foreign policy in the next two years, shape foreign-policy debates in the coming presidential primary, and allow the next commander in chief to confront the world as it will be in 2029.

With Democrats in decisive control of the 120th Congress, the time has come for the party to offer a vision for what comes next for U.S. foreign policy. The country’s stunning repudiation of U.S. President Donald Trump is stoking the temptation to embrace a sharp policy reversal, on the assumption that the center of American democracy has held and the pre-Trump foreign-policy consensus can, too. However, when it comes to working with U.S. allies, that would be a grave mistake.

The next Congress has an important role to play in defining this new foreign-policy vision—one that the next president could build upon in 2029. In asserting its powers to conduct oversight, legislate, and conduct its own diplomacy, the Democratic majority should be seeking to put in place elements of a new U.S. approach, rather than simply reverse the Trumpian damage. Doing so will begin to reorient U.S. foreign policy in the next two years, shape foreign-policy debates in the coming presidential primary, and allow the next commander in chief to confront the world as it will be in 2029.

The impulse to reverse course on Trump’s alliance policy is understandable. The president has brought two years of vitriol and abuse upon the United States’ closest friends—from a trade war with Canada to threats to invade Greenland—with clear strategic costs. But the flaws of his approach, and its broad unpopularity with the American public, are not a mandate for reflexive reversal. Nevertheless, there is a growing view in both Washington and allied capitals that, under new congressional leadership and with a new administration just two years away, Washington should take a maximally conciliatory approach to its friends. Apology tours, day-one tariff repeals, and the reinstatement of withdrawn troops in allied countries are all cited as necessary steps to regain lost trust.

The problem with that approach is twofold. First, it prioritizes rebuilding trust with allies over something more important—transforming old alliance bargains. The U.S. alliance system was built for the early Cold War world and used conventional and nuclear deterrence to keep threats far from the country’s shores. Its record of success is remarkable: No U.S. ally has ever been attacked, and U.S. treaty guarantees were invoked just once—on Washington’s behalf following the Sept. 11 attacks. But in the post-Cold War world, the United States and its allies need to cooperate on artificial intelligence, securing vital supply chains, aligning on climate and industrial policy, and combatting threats in cyberspace. Reembracing alliances without insisting on much-needed modernization would miss the chance to update them for new opportunities and threats, leaving the U.S. alliance network far less effective.

Reflexive policy reversal also ignores the ways in which allies approach the United States differently after Trump’s reelection and punitive second term. U.S. leadership on global issues is now constrained by a four-year problem. Having seen the United States succumb to political chaos twice in a decade at the expense of its own global position, friends and partners around the world will assume that any future deal they cut with the United States is only good for four years, until power changes hands again. If the United States wants close cooperation from allies in this world, then it will have to give them some space to build autonomy and resilience in case Washington defects again.

Taking this advice would prompt Democratic leaders to resist conventional wisdom on two issues in particular: tariffs and defense burden-sharing.

Trump’s trade war has proven to be both bad policy and bad politics, and it has hit U.S. allies as hard as its competitors. Many allies will argue that tariff reversals are an essential precondition for earning back their trust in the post-Trump era. But pursuing a unilateral, blanket repeal of tariffs on allies and partners—whether as an act of Congress or in the early days of a new administration—would be a mistake. Instead, Democrats can use their newfound control of Congress to check illegal tariffs that have driven up costs for American consumers, such as tariffs on forced labor, and repeal senseless duties on Canada. Such steps should pave the way for a broader international-economic agenda in 2029 that strengthens the U.S. economy and restores predictability for workers and businesses. That could start with plans to lower remaining tariffs on allies as part of a new economic bargain that includes bold, joint action against unfair Chinese trade practices and new agreements on technology and supply chain cooperation. Trump’s wanton tariff leverage should be parlayed into new cooperation, rather than freely ceded, to serve the bottom line of the American people and those in friendly nations.

A phased plan for tariffs also points the way for Democrats to take a new approach to allied burden-sharing on security and defense. Denouncing Trump’s abusive approach, elevating alliances as a strategic priority, and unambiguously acknowledging China and Russia as shared threats can begin to improve U.S. relationships. But congressional Democrats should not launch an apology tour or provide slavish reassurances that undercut the progress that allies have made toward better defending themselves. Instead, Democrats should encourage allies to continue investing in their own defense in Europe and Asia, and adjust U.S. policies to actively support these efforts, even if the United States loses some influence as allies take on a greater role. Following a disastrous war with Iran that has cratered U.S. defense stockpiles, Congress should fund super-charged efforts to coproduce munitions and other critical systems alongside allies to rebuild deterrence. And, notwithstanding the flawed process by which the Trump administration has approached its ongoing global force posture review, Democrats should bring an open mind to the strategic benefits of a rebalanced U.S. presence in some regions.

Newly empowered, Democrats should seize the opportunity to reassert allies as central to U.S. global strategy. But that should not mean a return to old patterns of burden-sharing, which too often let allies off the hook and created dependencies that they will no longer accept and the United States should not encourage. Nor should Washington fall back on traditional modes of collaboration, which privileged military commitments whose benefits may feel abstract and undervalued the economic and technological domains that most benefit Americans. The Trump shock to the U.S. alliance system has come with high costs, and most of this approach should be rejected. But Democrats should also identify where policies of the past two years have created new openings or new leverage and use those opportunities wisely, rather than giving them away for free. Rebuilding critical U.S. relationships is essential, but it is a long-term project. After two Trump presidencies, quick policy concessions will not overcome the structural sources of allied skepticism about U.S. reliability.

The world that the next U.S. president meets in 2029 will look dramatically different than the one of 2025 or 2021. The post-Cold War era has ended in a convulsion, and the Trump presidency, which has intentionally ravaged the United States’ global role, has two years of chaos remaining. Rather than attempt to run down the clock through 2028 and overturn his disastrous policies wholesale, congressional Democrats have a chance to build a policy bridge to a new era. By prioritizing the renovation and resilience in the U.S. global alliance system, Congress can work with—rather than in reflexive opposition to—the epochal global shifts that have taken place and position Washington to inaugurate a new era of global leadership in 2029.

Rebecca Lissner is a senior fellow for U.S. foreign policy and director of the Future of American Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations. She served as a deputy assistant to the president and principal deputy national security advisor to the vice president in the Biden-Harris administration. X: @RebeccaLissner

Mira Rapp-Hooper is a visiting senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. She was the senior director for East Asia and Oceania at the White House’s National Security Council from 2023-2025.
