#5896. How Xi Sees a Weakened Trump

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Analysis: How Xi Sees a Weakened Trump

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Voters dealt U.S. President Donald Trump a crushing rebuke in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, with Republicans losing control of both chambers of Congress. As Trump meets once again with Xi Jinping this week, how will the Chinese leader now view a weakened U.S. president?

I believe Xi will not fundamentally change his personal assessment of Trump. But he is reassessing Trump’s ability to shape U.S.-China relations over the next two years—and the extent to which the two leaders can deliver on the new framework for bilateral relations they agreed on this year. Beijing may come to see Trump as a president who remains willing to negotiate on a personal level but is becoming less capable of delivering on major political commitments.

Voters dealt U.S. President Donald Trump a crushing rebuke in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, with Republicans losing control of both chambers of Congress. As Trump meets once again with Xi Jinping this week, how will the Chinese leader now view a weakened U.S. president?

I believe Xi will not fundamentally change his personal assessment of Trump. But he is reassessing Trump’s ability to shape U.S.-China relations over the next two years—and the extent to which the two leaders can deliver on the new framework for bilateral relations they agreed on this year. Beijing may come to see Trump as a president who remains willing to negotiate on a personal level but is becoming less capable of delivering on major political commitments.

This matters because both Xi and Trump place considerable importance on personal diplomacy between heads of state. Trump visited China in May, and Xi traveled to the United States in September. During those meetings, according to the Chinese readout, they agreed to establish a new framework for bilateral relations: a “constructive and strategically stable relationship based on respect, fairness, and reciprocity.” Xi also called for a relationship characterized by “cooperation as the priority, managed competition, controlled differences, and the prospect of peace.”

Trump, for his part, repeatedly emphasized his good personal relationship with Xi and expressed confidence that U.S.-China relations could succeed under their leadership.

Despite their very different political backgrounds and governing philosophies, Xi and Trump, who have both sought to expand their own authority at home, share a belief that strong leaders can play a decisive role in national decision-making. Beijing routinely emphasizes the strategic importance of diplomacy conducted by heads of state. Trump, meanwhile, distrusts the traditional foreign-policy bureaucracy and prefers to negotiate deals directly with other leaders. Both seem to believe that once leaders reach an understanding, many complicated problems between their countries can be resolved.

But there is a fundamental difference between them. Xi’s autocratic status allows him to translate his personal diplomatic preferences into Chinese government policy. Trump, despite his unusually personal approach to presidential decision-making, cannot entirely circumvent Congress, the judiciary, or other domestic political forces—especially after the recent midterm results.

That difference was less visible when Republicans controlled both the White House and Congress. After returning to office, Trump enjoyed considerable authority within the Republican Party, while a supine Congress offered little effective resistance to his policies, even when pro-Ukrainian Republicans objected to his attempts to cozy up to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Xi had reason to believe that maintaining a stable personal relationship with Trump could help stabilize Washington’s China policy and perhaps even facilitate adjustments to U.S. positions on sensitive issues through direct negotiations between the two leaders.

The midterms have changed that. With Democrats controlling Congress, Trump retains substantial authority over foreign affairs, but major agreements he reaches with Xi will face greater congressional scrutiny and potential challenges. On Taiwan and advanced technology in particular, especially after the Jensen Huang scandal, Democrats are not necessarily more accommodating toward China than Republicans. If Trump attempts to make significant concessions to Beijing in these areas, Democrats could use hearings, investigations, budgetary powers, and legislation to obstruct him—and turn any such concessions into political ammunition.

For Trump, however, the more difficult constraint may come from his own party’s political interests. He cannot run for president again, however much he wants to, but Republicans must defend the White House and seek to regain Congress in 2028. If Democrats portray a Trump-Xi agreement as sacrificing Taiwan’s security or undermining America’s technological advantage, Republican candidates will face an uncomfortable choice. Supporting Trump could expose them to accusations of being soft on China; opposing him could alienate MAGA voters. Trump may be willing to disregard Democratic criticism, but he cannot entirely ignore his party’s electoral prospects or his own political legacy.

This creates a paradox. Having lost his congressional majority, Trump may have a stronger incentive to demonstrate his leadership through foreign-policy achievements, making him more eager to reach a major agreement with Xi. Yet the greater his need to present such an agreement as a victory for the United States, the less room he has to appear to be making concessions to China. His weakened political position increases his incentive to strike a deal while simultaneously narrowing the concessions he can offer.

Xi is likely to recognize this. Rather than downgrading the importance of his personal relationship with Trump, he may become even more determined to preserve that direct channel of communication. Compared with Democratic politicians, Trump remains more inclined to approach U.S.-China relations transactionally and more willing to adjust specific policies according to his own judgment. From Chinese leaders’ perspective, he remains someone they can deal with—but they may no longer trust his ability to deliver. He remains a president worth negotiating with.

Beijing set the language after the Trump-Xi meeting in September, with little pushback from the White House. From Beijing’s perspective, the framework represents more than an effort to move beyond the intense trade confrontation of recent years. It also signals, in China’s interpretation, that Washington is beginning to accept China as an equal strategic power and is willing to keep bilateral competition within certain limits. Beijing clearly hopes that the principles of “respect” and “strategic stability” will extend to issues it considers central to its interests, particularly Taiwan and technology.

Yet Trump’s acceptance of this diplomatic language does not mean the entire U.S. political system is on board. Trump himself may well not understand the implications of the Chinese language. For Washington, strategic stability is more about managing conflict, protecting U.S. interests, and preserving competitive advantages.

The Chinese Foreign Ministry’s response to the results of the U.S. midterms offers an indication of Beijing’s approach. Rather than commenting on Trump’s political defeat, its spokesperson emphasized China’s willingness to continue implementing the understandings reached by the two presidents and to advance their constructive, strategically stable relationship.

Xi is unlikely to repudiate diplomatic achievements in which he has invested substantial political capital simply because of a U.S. midterm election. On the contrary, he has good reason to reaffirm the framework and invoke it when pressing Washington to honor the understandings reached between the two leaders.

But I suspect that the more Beijing emphasizes the framework in its diplomatic rhetoric, the more cautious it will become in practice. This brings us to a second question: How does Xi interpret U.S. politics itself?

When Trump won reelection in 2024, Republicans also captured both chambers of Congress, and the media was eager to trumpet a new era of dominant Trumpism. Just two years later, Democrats have won their biggest victory in generations. This sharp reversal may reinforce Xi’s perception that U.S. politics lacks stability and continuity.

Yet Xi would be making a mistake if he interpreted U.S. political divisions as evidence that China now enjoys a greater strategic opportunity. In U.S. politics, the two parties may fight bitterly over domestic issues and presidential authority while maintaining considerable agreement on strategic competition with China.

I expect Beijing to gradually shift the emphasis of its U.S. policy over the next two years. It will continue to maintain Xi’s personal relationship with Trump, seek to implement existing agreements, and avoid another serious confrontation over trade or security. At the same time, it will lower its expectations that leader-to-leader diplomacy can fundamentally redirect U.S.-China relations. Instead, Beijing will accelerate attempts to reduce China’s vulnerability to shifts in U.S. policy during a prolonged period of strategic competition.

Such an adjustment would not mean Xi is preparing for an all-out confrontation with the United States. Because Beijing increasingly recognizes that the competition will be prolonged, it has greater reason to avoid a direct clash before the conditions are in its failure. Maintaining basic stability in U.S.-China relations remains a way to buy time for China’s own development.

The new framework established by Xi and Trump this year is therefore unlikely to be abandoned easily. Beijing still needs it, and so does Trump. But their expectations may increasingly diverge. Xi wants the framework to provide China with long-term strategic stability, while Trump is more likely to see it as a means of managing relations with Beijing and securing diplomatic achievements during the remainder of his presidency.

For Xi, the central lesson of the midterms may be that he can build personal trust with Trump but he cannot entrust the future of U.S.-China relations to Trump alone.

Deng Yuwen is a Chinese writer and scholar.

Analysis: Japan’s Defense Lessons From Ukraine and the Middle East

Since taking office in October 2025, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has been busy reforming Japan’s defense policy. Her government is revising the National Security Strategy, National Defense Strategy, and Defense Buildup Program to prepare for an era of heightened instability and growing uncertainty over U.S. engagement in the region. Notably, Tokyo raised defense and other security-related spending to approximately 1.8 percent of GDP in the 2025-2026fiscal year, up from around 1 percent in 2022. In April, Japan also revised its defense transfer policy with the aim of promoting exports of weapons and nonlethal military equipment.

Expanding Japan’s defense production capacity has been a central focus of these reforms. In its budget request for the 2027 fiscal year, the Japanese Defense Ministry singles out domestic military production as a critical element of deterrence. This reflects growing concerns that Japan may need to sustain military operations in a protracted, high-intensity conflict. In an analysis of the U.S.-Israel war against Iran that was published in August, the Defense Ministry explicitly recognizes the need to maintain adequate production capacity in peacetime—and to be ready to rapidly scale up weapons production in the event of a conflict.

Since taking office in October 2025, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has been busy reforming Japan’s defense policy. Her government is revising the National Security Strategy, National Defense Strategy, and Defense Buildup Program to prepare for an era of heightened instability and growing uncertainty over U.S. engagement in the region. Notably, Tokyo raised defense and other security-related spending to approximately 1.8 percent of GDP in the 2025-2026fiscal year, up from around 1 percent in 2022. In April, Japan also revised its defense transfer policy with the aim of promoting exports of weapons and nonlethal military equipment.

Expanding Japan’s defense production capacity has been a central focus of these reforms. In its budget request for the 2027 fiscal year, the Japanese Defense Ministry singles out domestic military production as a critical element of deterrence. This reflects growing concerns that Japan may need to sustain military operations in a protracted, high-intensity conflict. In an analysis of the U.S.-Israel war against Iran that was published in August, the Defense Ministry explicitly recognizes the need to maintain adequate production capacity in peacetime—and to be ready to rapidly scale up weapons production in the event of a conflict.

Japan’s focus on production capacity reflects a change in the way that military planners think about deterrence. Russia’s yearslong war against Ukraine and the ongoing conflict in the Middle East have demonstrated the prolonged, high-intensity, resource-draining nature of modern warfare. Some analysts now expect a potential conflict over Taiwan to play out in similar ways, rather than the quick, decisive campaign that many experts had long assumed as their base case.

NATO frames deterrence around three elements: capability (does a state have the weapons to defend itself?), credibility (would it actually use them?), and communication (does the adversary understand what it would be up against?). In a long, high-intensity conflict, each of these three pillars is increasingly shaped by production capacity.

Production capacity affects the availability of the weapons needed for military operations both in preparation during peacetime and during an ongoing war. Recent conflicts have underlined two aspects of replenishment capability: the replacement rate (whether weapons output keeps pace with consumption in the battlespace) and the cost-to-kill ratio (how much a defensive weapon costs compared to the offensive threat that it counters).

In terms of credibility, a longer conflict is not just about the willingness to use force but also the willingness to sustain it for the duration of the conflict. The durability of public and private investment signals whether a state can support production throughout a prolonged conflict.

In terms of communication, an adversary’s calculation—and hence the deterrent effect—is affected by the signal sent by investing political and financial capital in defense production capacity.

Viewed through this framework, recent announcements by the Japanese government and reports on the forthcoming reforms show how production capacity relates to the three pillars of deterrence. To upgrade capability, Tokyo has indicated that it will accelerate support for domestic industry. To this end, the Japanese government is planning to release a new defense industrial base strategy, likely to include new subsidies to support defense firms’ production capacity. One plan is to extend an existing scheme to the acquisition and maintenance of production facilities for ammunition and other critical supplies necessary for sustained combat capability. Through greater governmental support, Tokyo aims to establish spare defense production capacity that could sustain protracted and high-intensity warfare.

To enhance credibility—by demonstrating willingness not just to spend now but also to keep spending in the future—Tokyo is working to bolster the domestic defense investment landscape. Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi has urged Japanese financial institutions to provide investment and loans to grow the domestic defense sector, and lenders are responding.

In May, the Development Bank of Japan, a state-owned institution, eased its restrictions on financing domestic arms manufacturers. Private banks are also increasing their involvement in the sector. MUFG Bank, one of Japan’s largest private-sector banks, is reportedly planning to establish criteria for lending to defense-related companies after having previously been cautious. These measures normalize defense-related investments in peacetime, but they do not guarantee the financial sector’s commitment to invest in case of a longer conflict.

In April, the Defense Ministry stated that Japan must not allow an adversary to believe that prolonging a conflict would ensure the success of an invasion, emphasizing the importance of stockpiling and domestic production. Koizumi has made the connection between defense production and deterrence increasingly explicit. Economy, Trade and Industry Minister Ryosei Akazawa has also been explicit about investing in the industrial base for dual-use goods in order to strengthen Japan’s ability to sustain military operations.

In terms of communicating deterrence, Tokyo is matching these efforts with political signaling that its new defense-industrial posture is a long-term change that’s here to stay.

There are still two major gaps in Japan’s production planning for a potential conflict. First—despite these initiatives—Japan is still struggling to ramp up defense production. According to the Defense Ministry’s assessments, insufficient parts production is likely to continue limiting the operational availability of military equipment, particularly aircraft, for the Japanese Self-Defense Forces.

This means that Japan is still struggling to meet peacetime demand, let alone the surge in production that a protracted conflict would require. Tokyo is considering government-owned, contractor-operated facilities as a means to enable rapid defense production increases when needed, but the feasibility and potential scale of such agreements remain unclear. This problem is exacerbated by the absence of a legal framework that would allow the government to compel manufacturers to sustain operations in wartime, raising fundamental questions about Tokyo’s ability to translate expanded capacity into wartime output.

Second, Japan’s defense supply chain remains vulnerable. It is extensive and stretched thin, including around 1,100 manufacturers involved in the production of fighter jets, 1,300 for tanks, and 8,300 for destroyers. Despite Tokyo’s efforts to enhance its defense capability, protecting this extensive network remains challenging. In many cases, it is difficult to find alternative suppliers for specialized component materials or specific manufacturing processes. Consequently, disruption to any part of the supply chain could affect the stable supply and maintenance of equipment.

Strengthening supply-chain resilience, particularly with regard to small and medium suppliers, is crucial to ensuring a stable supply of equipment. Tokyo is considering dispersing, hardening, and placing military facilities underground, but these discussions do not apply to industrial suppliers. Increasing supply-chain redundancy—both domestically and with Japan’s strategic partners—is also critical.

In this respect, the deal with Australia for upgraded Mogami-class frigates, as well as discussions with Indonesia on transferring used Asagiri-class destroyers there, include cooperation on maintenance. Foreign-based maintenance facilities for Japanese-built platforms could, over time, provide additional repair capacity outside Japan.

The revision of Japan’s three national strategic documents and the Defense Industry Policy is expected to be concluded next month. The policies set out in these documents will determine the course of Japan’s defense industrial policy in the years to come. If production capacity in a protracted conflict is now part of Tokyo’s deterrence calculations, then the test for the strategy documents to be released in December will be whether they move beyond only peacetime capacity. This would entail granting the government the authority to direct production during wartime and planning how civilian manufacturers, particularly in dual-use sectors, could contribute to a wartime surge. Alongside these policies, effective strategic communication to shape an adversary’s expectations about the duration and likely outcome of a conflict will be key to strengthening deterrence.

Jumpei Ishimaru is a research analyst in the Japan program at the International Institute for Strategic Studies.

#5892. A Diminished Trump Could Get Played in Asia

Argument: A Diminished Trump Could Get Played in Asia

When U.S. President Donald Trump touches down in Shenzhen, China, this week for a three-way summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, he will be embarking on the highest-level diplomacy he has ever undertaken at his weakest point in power.

The problem is not merely the devastating midterm election losses for his Republican Party, in which he urged supporters to turn out and cast their votes as if he were on the ballot. In recent weeks, Trump has displayed startling new levels of incoherence and evasion of responsibility for a sitting president. This seemed to reach a crescendo last week with two national crises for which Trump had no suitable answers.

When U.S. President Donald Trump touches down in Shenzhen, China, this week for a three-way summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, he will be embarking on the highest-level diplomacy he has ever undertaken at his weakest point in power.

The problem is not merely the devastating midterm election losses for his Republican Party, in which he urged supporters to turn out and cast their votes as if he were on the ballot. In recent weeks, Trump has displayed startling new levels of incoherence and evasion of responsibility for a sitting president. This seemed to reach a crescendo last week with two national crises for which Trump had no suitable answers.

The first of these crises brought news that Jensen Huang, the head of Nvidia, at once one of the world’s most valuable and strategically important companies, had had an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Trump pleaded ignorance, denying well-sourced reports that he had been briefed about the matter as long ago as May, including by his national security advisor and secretary of state, Marco Rubio. The only thoughts the president seemed able to summon reflected credulity about Huang’s claim that he had never suspected the woman could have been a spy and personal sympathy for a man who had, until his sudden resignation from Nvidia last week, belonged to a club that means more to Trump than any other: the exclusive circle of the world’s richest and most powerful men. Perhaps for that reason, on Monday, Trump told reporters he “would not mind” if Huang was reinstated.

For all of Trump’s envy of powerful authoritarians, if the situations were reversed and Huang were a Chinese national leading a company as important as Nvidia, it is impossible to imagine Xi treating a man under such suspicions this way, including welcoming him on a flight to his country’s No. 1 competitor and adversary. But Trump’s need for this kind of validation is an ongoing matter and not something he has learned a lesson from. Witness his decision to invite the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, to join him on this trip, if not in the meetings with his fellow heads of state.

For a U.S. president heading off to a summit such as this, the week’s second crisis may have been even worse. The image the United States presented to the world in the wake of a breakdown in the nationwide air traffic control system on Friday was one of utter dishevelment and incompetence. It put the spotlight on two of arguably the least qualified members of a cabinet resolutely hostile to meritocracy: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, a former congressman and Fox News personality, and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, a former congressman whose formal education culminated with an associate’s degree in plumbing and construction.

With thousands of flights canceled and a country desperate for answers and reassurance, they bumbled their way through an almost incoherent news conference that offered no real explanations. Instead, they cast blame on others, including Congress and past administrations, while exalting Trump’s leadership as if they were members of a personality cult and the public should be too. During the first 36 hours of the crisis, Trump for his part chose to lie low, making no statements about the matter, apparently fearing that doing so would mean taking responsibility for something bad that happened on his watch, which he has always been deeply allergic to.

The U.S. president will visit the Philippines and China fresh off his party’s midterm defeat.

Political instability is more danger than opportunity for Beijing.

The Nvidia scandal could upend a fragile consensus in Washington.

These displays of unaccountable behavior and cluelessness are bad enough for the United States in their own right, but Americans should be worried about their implications for the upcoming summit. Even in ordinary times, Trump’s narcissism and emotional neediness make diplomacy like this dangerous because he craves fellowship and approval from men such as Putin and Xi, whom he all but openly idolizes. But with last week’s crises and domestic scandals sprouting in many directions as Democrats prepare to take over Congress, Trump is liable to make large and unwise concessions to his imagined peers in order to secure political coups that he hopes can restore prestige and momentum to his badly weakened presidency. The cliché holds that weakened or trapped animals are liable to strike out to defend themselves. With Trump, the danger is the opposite—given his self-centered view of the world, where his own ego gratification is paramount, he could give away the store.

What could that mean? Here, one feels that Trump is so easily flattered that the sky is almost the limit. He has reportedly already forsworn raising the Nvidia crisis with Xi as well as Russia’s ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine. If true, such self-imposed restrictions themselves emphasize the weakness of the U.S. president’s hand and preemptively vitiate the utility of such an unusual gathering.

What does this leave on the table for discussion? The Trump administration has said it hopes to make progress on limiting nuclear weapons armament at a time when the United States and Russia still have enormous legacy arsenals whose maintenance and modernization are costly and China is belatedly racing to catch up. Trump officials have also said they hope to engage leaders of the world’s other two big powers on the United States’ stop-and-go war against Iran, which by now has turned into a quagmire.

But what could the latter possibly yield? That Trump has already displayed weakness and enormous gullibility on Iran in his dealings with both powers does not bode well. Russia has supplied intelligence and munitions support to Iran throughout the war, enabling that country to target U.S. military bases throughout the Middle East with devastating effect. Consistent with his general enthrallment to Putin, Trump has publicly downplayed the importance of this, making clear that maintaining warm relations with Moscow is his priority. China, if more cautious than Russia, has also hewed to a line that has enhanced the Iranian state’s position. It has done this by continuing to purchase as much Iranian oil as it can while also reportedly supplying electronic components essential to that country’s missile and drone production. Genuine progress toward administration goals on Iran would require concrete commitments from both powers to stop what they are currently doing. Trump appears unlikely to demand this, and even if he did, neither is likely to follow through.

Putin has already mesmerized Trump into treating Ukraine as if it were the faulty party in its defensive war against Russia. That conflict may not officially be on the agenda when the three leaders sit down together on Thursday, but the specific danger in Shenzhen is that Putin will offer Trump a vague, unverifiable promise to limit support for Iran—something that Trump can present as a win—in exchange for Trump’s deeper complicity in ending the Ukraine war on Russian terms. It would be a trade of something real and irreversible for something hollow and unenforceable. Because of Trump’s unique weakness for glad-handing and grandiosity, it may take little more than that. A more lucid and competent U.S. president would never allow such confusion between the two crises.

What might Xi seek, and how do Trump’s growing vulnerabilities play into this? Beijing’s biggest goal is progress toward exerting control over Taiwan, if not taking over the island altogether by the eventual end of Xi’s longtime hold on power. Toward this end, Trump has already gifted Xi in important ways without receiving anything in return. At the level of official rhetoric, Trump has weakened America’s traditional support for a peaceful resolution of the dispute between Beijing and Taipei over the island’s future. In fact, he has come close to saying the United States would have no business defending Taiwan in case a war broke out between the two sides.

This by itself is an immense gift, and it would be enhanced further if Trump delayed arms sales to Taiwan to ingratiate himself with Xi. Already, the U.S. military posture in East Asia has been dramatically weakened by the prolonged deployment of aircraft carrier battle groups near Iran and by heavy depletion of advanced weapons systems during the war with that country. Trump has also weakened U.S. alliances in Asia through tariff demands and unpredictable behavior. By nature, Xi seems much more cautious than Putin. But sensing Trump’s weakness and need for some kind of foreign-policy achievement, however illusory, he could try to induce concessions through displays of strongman camaraderie and vague pledges of cooperation in areas of U.S. need.

If we cannot know in advance what these meetings will produce, we should know one thing already. Trump will emerge from them making great claims about how well he gets along with the world’s two other most powerful heads of state. In fact, nothing more might publicly come out of the meetings beyond this. But the world should be wary even of any quiet understandings that Trump, at this moment of extreme weakness and vulnerability, believes he has reached. The likelihood is that he is being played due to his personal and political need, and if the details are unknowable, the costs could be great.

Howard W. French is a columnist at Foreign Policy, a professor at the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism, and a longtime foreign correspondent. His latest book is The Second Emancipation: Nkrumah, Pan-Africanism, and Global Blackness at High Tide. Bluesky: @hofrench.bsky.social X: @hofrench

#5891. Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

Outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

Zinke’s wife, son, and sister currently serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

In a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he said when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke said.

None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

“While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” said Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Issue One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

“I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” said Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

“Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he said, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

Zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

It marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

The Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with plans to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

Zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services company Halliburton.

Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

Supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a company registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron said.

Since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s company, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which says it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

“We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he said, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

In 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

“If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail said about SEAL PAC's payments.

But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

#5889. Engine failure forces Sen Ashley Moody’s American Airlines flight to divert for emergency landing

An American Airlines flight carrying Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla., was diverted to Orlando after a reported engine failure. (Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

An American Airlines flight carrying Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla., was diverted to Orlando after a reported engine failure, according to a spokesperson for the senator's office.

American Airlines Flight 496 was heading from Tampa to Washington, D.C., when it was forced to divert to Orlando.

Moody missed Senate votes on Monday night due to the incident, but the aircraft landed safely, her office said.

#5888. Trump arrives in Philippines ahead of Xi Jinping summit in China after GOP midterm losses

Fox News' Mark Meredith reports the latest on his visit from Manila. The Heritage Foundation's Victoria Coates also weighs in on the trip during 'Fox & Friends First.'

President Donald Trump touched down in the Philippines on Tuesday as part of an Asia trip that will take him to China for a historic summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The trip marks Trump's first overseas visit since Republicans suffered bruising defeats in the U.S. midterm elections.

Trump noted during a gaggle on Monday that while in China this week he will meet with Chinese President Xi Jingping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

TRUMP BRINGS TWO DIVIDED CABINET HEAVYWEIGHTS TO CHINA AS CONTROVERSY HANGS OVER HIGH-STAKES TALKS

President Donald Trump boards Air Force One on Nov. 16, 2026, at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

"And then we go to China. And we'll be with President Xi, he was here a month ago. And we're also gonna meet with President Putin. And we may meet with Kim Jong Un also," Trump said, referring to North Korea's leader. "He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi," Trump later added.

Trump indicated that during the meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts, they would discuss issues including denuclearization, Iran, Ukraine, economics and trade.

Asked on Tuesday if Kim Jong Un would come, Trump said, "He would like to, yeah. We'll see what happens.

The trip also comes after tech giant Nvidia announced last week that President and CEO Jensen Huang had resigned from the company — the resignation announcement was made after Huang admitted to cheating on his wife amid reporting that he had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

TRUMP'S ASIA TRIP TAKES ALASKA DETOUR AS WEATHER FORCES REFUELING STOP CHANGE

US President Donald Trump waves U.S. and Philippine flags as he arrives at Ninoy Aquino International Airport to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila on Nov. 17, 2026. (Eloisa Lopez/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Trump met Tuesday in the Philippines with leaders of the Quad, which includes the U.S., Japan, Australia and India.

He signed a document with Thailand Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul on Tuesday as the two nations moved closer toward inking a trade deal.

"Today's deal lays the foundation for much stronger trading relationship that will bring the United States and Thailand closer than ever before," Trump said.

"Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on U.S. exports ... and remove substantial non-tariff barriers on American vehicles, medical devices, pharmaceuticals, ethanol and poultry. Thailand will also be buying an estimated $2.6 billion in additional U.S. agricultural products," he said.

"This is an incredible victory for both countries, both the people of Thailand and the American people. And I look forward to finalizing the details of our formal agreement in the coming weeks," Trump said, noting that today they were signing "a joint statement talking about the deal," which will eventually be finalized.

"Actually, it's a very big trade deal," Trump later said.

The title on the document they signed reads, "Joint Statement on an Agreement Between the United States of America and the Kingdom of Thailand on Reciprocal Trade." The statement says that the two men "have reached substantial conclusion in their negotiations" toward a trade agreement.

UKRAINE HITS PUTIN'S PRIZED BRIDGE IN RECORD DRONE BLITZ AS KREMLIN TELLS LAWMAKERS TO PREPARE FOR ‘VICTORY’

President Donald Trump gestures upon arriving at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila on Nov. 17, 2026. (Eloisa Lopez/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Trump also addressed world leaders during an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) gathering in the Philippines on Tuesday.

"The United States is a Pacific nation in a true sense. And we have been engaged in trade and commerce and diplomacy across Southeast Asia for hundreds of years," Trump said. "I'm here today because America is deeply committed to the success, sovereignty and prosperity of our many friends and partners — many of whom are at this table right now — but partners in this region, and we always will be, we're with you always," he noted.

Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

#5887. The Middle East Is Finally on Its Own

Argument: The Middle East Is Finally on Its Own

According to Steve Simon, Washington’s dreams of “transforming” the Middle East have failed in the past, are failing today, and, if we continue them, will keep failing. He’s right, but I don’t think that we will continue these efforts, and neither will anyone else. On the contrary, we are approaching the end of a century or more in which outside powers drove events in the region even when they couldn’t achieve their main goals. For the first time since 1919, what happens there will be primarily determined by the local actors themselves. The failed U.S.-Israeli war against Iran is a watershed event, but it is merely accelerating developments that have been apparent for some time. Increasingly, states in the Middle East are going to be on their own.

The modern Middle East was heavily shaped by outside great powers. The victorious World War I allies carved new states out of the collapsing Ottoman Empire at the Paris Peace Conference in 1919, after making a lot of contradictory promises to various contenders during the war itself. Britain and France governed what is now Lebanon, Iraq, Israel, Syria, and Jordan for most of the interwar period, under mandates from the League of Nations, but the local inhabitants were increasingly restive even before World War II broke out and made it impossible for European powers to retain control. Saudi Arabia gained independence on its own, while Britain provided security for the smaller states in the Gulf. Active support from various outside powers—and especially the United States—was instrumental in Israel’s creation in 1948. Britain and the United States connived to topple the democratic government of Iran in 1953. And the Soviet decision to send arms to Egypt and Syria in the mid-1950s helped cause the 1956 Suez crisis and made the Middle East a central arena in the Cold War.

According to Steve Simon, Washington’s dreams of “transforming” the Middle East have failed in the past, are failing today, and, if we continue them, will keep failing. He’s right, but I don’t think that we will continue these efforts, and neither will anyone else. On the contrary, we are approaching the end of a century or more in which outside powers drove events in the region even when they couldn’t achieve their main goals. For the first time since 1919, what happens there will be primarily determined by the local actors themselves. The failed U.S.-Israeli war against Iran is a watershed event, but it is merely accelerating developments that have been apparent for some time. Increasingly, states in the Middle East are going to be on their own.

The modern Middle East was heavily shaped by outside great powers. The victorious World War I allies carved new states out of the collapsing Ottoman Empire at the Paris Peace Conference in 1919, after making a lot of contradictory promises to various contenders during the war itself. Britain and France governed what is now Lebanon, Iraq, Israel, Syria, and Jordan for most of the interwar period, under mandates from the League of Nations, but the local inhabitants were increasingly restive even before World War II broke out and made it impossible for European powers to retain control. Saudi Arabia gained independence on its own, while Britain provided security for the smaller states in the Gulf. Active support from various outside powers—and especially the United States—was instrumental in Israel’s creation in 1948. Britain and the United States connived to topple the democratic government of Iran in 1953. And the Soviet decision to send arms to Egypt and Syria in the mid-1950s helped cause the 1956 Suez crisis and made the Middle East a central arena in the Cold War.

For the next 35 years, the United States and Soviet Union armed their respective clients, toppled (or tried to topple) regimes they perceived as hostile, and sometimes intervened directly, albeit in mostly limited ways and only for short periods. The United States and USSR also worked together to impose cease-fires to end the recurring wars between Israel and its neighbors, but joint efforts to fashion a broader regional peace were consistently sacrificed on the altar of great-power rivalry.

The end of the Cold War didn’t end great-power meddling, but now it was the United States acting on its own. The first Bush administration organized the coalition that expelled Iraq from Kuwait in 1991, sponsored the Madrid Conference of 1991, took charge of (and mismanaged) the Oslo peace process, adopted a strategy of dual containment that helped pave the road to the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, and then tried to transform the entire region by toppling Saddam Hussein in 2003. We all know how that misguided adventure turned out. U.S. President Donald Trump’s current war with Iran can be seen the last gasp of this hubristic endeavor, with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu acting as cheerleader, a role he first assumed in 2002. (Regrettably, his forecasts back then were no better than his predictions in 2026).

Like a flash of lightning, the war with Iran has illuminated the new strategic landscape. The failed U.S. interventions in Iraq and Libya (along with Russia’s inability to prevent the eventual toppling of Syrian leader Bashar al-Assad) reveals new limits to what outside military power can accomplish. Similarly, Iran’s ability to resist decades of U.S. pressure and acquire a large arsenal of missiles and drones, plus mastery of the nuclear fuel cycle, further underscore the declining efficacy of outside intervention. Saudi Arabia’s lavishly funded military couldn’t bomb its way to victory over the Houthis in Yemen, and Israel’s repeated and increasingly ferocious assaults against its various opponents did not prevent Hamas from mounting a major attack in October 2023 or fully eliminate either Hamas or Hezbollah. Even before the war with Iran, in short, the limits of military power (and especially when wielded by states outside the region) were becoming clear.

Today, the combination of cheap but lethal drones and more sophisticated ballistic missiles has raised the cost of external military intervention to new heights. Not only did weeks of punishing air strikes fail to topple Iran’s regime, but the United States proved unable to protect its own bases in the region from Iranian retaliation. The damage to these facilities has made sustained military action in the region more difficult and expensive; for example, U.S. aircraft carriers cannot safely operate close to Iran, which reduces loiter times for attack aircraft and the payloads they can carry. Nor can the United States protect its local clients from being attacked, except by using lots of expensive interceptors (e.g. Patriot missiles) that are far more expensive than the missiles and drones they are shooting down and are in increasingly short supply. Nor are Patriots or systems like Israel’s Iron Dome impenetrable, especially when an adversary can fire lots of drones or missiles at once.

The limits of airpower have been apparent for a long time (although that reality is often ignored by political leaders eager to “do something”), but these new technologies are also making ground invasions increasingly unattractive. As we have seen in Ukraine, assembling large ground units exposes them to deadly drone or missile strikes, which is why loose talk about the United States invading Iran is not to be taken seriously. Iran may be deeply divided, and its government may be unpopular, but the occupations of Iraq and Afghanistan should have taught Americans by now that trying to invade and control a country of 80 million people is a very bad idea.

The bottom line is that the days when mighty great powers could intervene in the Middle East with near-impunity—as the United States did during Desert Storm in 1991—are behind us.

A second trend—the declining importance of Middle East energy—will reinforce the first. That might seem like an odd statement at present, given the sharp rise in fuel prices caused by the war, but most of these price rises are due to limited refining capacity (a problem exacerbated by the Iran war and the war in Ukraine) and not the supply of crude oil itself. The relative importance of Middle East energy has been declining significantly since 1973, when a Saudi-led boycott sent prices soaring and led to long gas lines in the United States. Since then, the shale oil boom in the United States and broader global efforts to address climate change by reducing fossil fuel consumption have made Middle East oil less critical than it used to be. That is why Middle Eastern countries like Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates are trying to diversify their own economies. They know that the days of oil and gas exports being able to pay all the bills are rapidly waning.

Note: I am not saying that energy (and fertilizer) supplies from the Middle East will be irrelevant, only that they will be much less critical in the future than they have been in the past. In short, the need to intervene in the region to safeguard energy exports is declining while the cost of trying to do so is rising. Put these two trends together, and direct military involvement by outside powers is much less attractive.

For the first time in more than a century, therefore, one can envision a Middle East whose fate is determined primarily by the peoples in the region and not by outsiders. Distant great powers will still have dealings with different Middle East states (such as selling arms, pursuing investments and trade arrangements, etc.) but local governments will have the initiative. What should we expect them to do?

For starters, I’d expect a lot of good, old-fashioned balance-of-power politics, where ideologies and sectarian differences matter little and the need to keep the strongest powers in check will drive an ever-shifting array of regional coalitions. At the same time, such a pattern does not preclude renewed efforts to lower tensions between Iran, Saudi Arabia, the Gulf states, and others, and perhaps even to negotiate a broader security architecture for the region that doesn’t depend on great-power support. The United States will revert to its former role as an “offshore balancer,” reduce its military footprint there, and pursue more businesslike relations with everyone in the region instead of “special relationships” with a few. In other words, it will act more like China. And if outside powers are no longer willing or able to provide protection, then more Middle Eastern states will be tempted to acquire a nuclear deterrent and the risk of preventive wars to thwart such efforts is likely to grow, as well.

One can also speculate on how these developments will affect the internal politics of some of these states. If Middle Eastern countries must rely primarily on their own resources and strategies for security and defense, they will have to get better at mobilizing real military power instead of just buying a lot of expensive toys from foreign defense contractors. But as King Farouk of Egypt or King Feisal II of Iraq could have told you, creating more potent military forces is risky in top-down societies ruled by privileged elites, because the guardians of their power may want more of a say in how things are run. For this reason, the emergence of a more autonomous Middle East could also usher in a new era of internal political turmoil.

The bottom line: We may be approaching the end of foreign efforts to remake the Middle East, but don’t expect the region to become boring.

Stephen M. Walt is a columnist at Foreign Policy and the Robert and Renée Belfer professor of international relations at Harvard University. Walt is the author of The New Geopolitics, a five-part newsletter masterclass breaking down the biggest concepts you should use to navigate today’s world. #5886. Now hiring: Staff to power Democrats’ probes

Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.

That means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

Arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, said the pressure will be on from day one.

“Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan said.

Still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she says of staffers headed there for the first time.

The work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can quickly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

Some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

There’s every indication that pressure will continue in the new Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, said Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

“Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres said.

Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the new year, if they haven’t already, Melendres said.

“There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he said.

In addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the new Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

“For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a big part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres said.

Lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a big difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

For instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

Standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

Those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, said he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the new Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

“But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin said.

The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”

Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

“The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren said.

Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal said he won’t be deterred by the letter.

“There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” said Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”

“I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

“We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries said.

Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

Beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet announced — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

In prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

“I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin said.

#5885. Trump kicks off high-stakes Asia trip with Xi, Putin meetings looming on world stage

Former State Department senior advisor Christian Whiton joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to discuss President Donald Trump's upcoming summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Whiton breaks down the potential for nuclear arms agreements, ongoing trade negotiations and the shifting geopolitical dynamics between the U.S., Russia and China.

President Donald Trump is in Asia for historic talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin this week, with nuclear arms reductions and Iran on the agenda and Trump signaling Monday that he also plans to raise Russia's war in Ukraine.

Trump's trip began Tuesday in the Philippines at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit before he travels to Shenzhen, China, for Thursday's meeting with Xi and Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

The rare gathering comes amid simmering U.S.-China trade tensions and ongoing conflicts involving Russia and Iran, with Trump signaling plans to raise denuclearization and efforts to end the fighting.

At the ASEAN summit, Trump is expected to sign a joint statement with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul announcing progress toward a trade agreement. The president is also set to meet with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. before departing for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China.

TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA

President Donald Trump shakes hands with Chinese President Xi Jinping as they hold a bilateral meeting at Gimhae International Airport, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, in Busan, South Korea, on Oct. 30, 2025. (Reuters/Evelyn Hockstein)

The president has also raised the possibility of meeting with North Korean dictator Kim Jong-un during his visit to China this week, telling reporters Monday that talks could take place.

When reached for additional comment about the floated meeting, the White House referred Fox News Digital to Trump's remarks to reporters on Monday.

Trump is expected to discuss Iran and Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin during Thursday's highly-anticipated trilateral meeting, despite U.S. officials previously telling ABC News that Ukraine likely would not be on the agenda.

Trump notably told reporters on Nov. 8 that he plans to discuss denuclearization and ending the war in Iran during the trilateral meeting, DW News reported.

"We'll talk a lot of things, including denuclearization, but we'll be talking a lot of things. We're trying to end the war in Iran," the president said at the time.

From right to left, President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping at Gimhae International Airport in Busan, South Korea, Thursday, Oct. 30, 2025. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)

Trump's trip also comes amid a scandal involving Nvidia, the American tech giant whose powerful AI chips are at the center of growing tensions between the U.S. and China.

Nvidia's former CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned last week following reports of an affair with a woman suspected by U.S. intelligence officials of sharing information with Beijing, raising fresh concerns about Chinese espionage and access to sensitive American technology.

Trump cast doubt on the espionage allegations Monday, telling reporters he was unsure whether the woman was a Chinese spy. He also said he would be open to Huang returning as CEO.

TRUMP-XI REUNION COMES WITH UNFINISHED BUSINESS — AND A BIGGER BATTLE LOOMING

President Donald Trump greets Russian President Vladimir Putin on the tarmac after they arrived at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Anchorage, Alaska, on August 15, 2025. (Photo by Andrew Cabellero-Reynolds/AFP)

The president will be joined by several high-profile figures during his Asia trip, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is accompanying Trump to the Philippines and China this week, according to Rubio's public schedule.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk is also expected to join Trump for part of his trip to China for the APEC summit, U.S. officials confirmed to CNBC on Friday.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chairman of the House Select Committee on Strategic Competition between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party, told CBS News’ "Face the Nation" in an interview on Sunday that he does not anticipate any agreements related to the reduction of nuclear weapons will be made this week.

"I don’t believe any agreements are going to be made, but certainly China has resisted being part of any agreements," Moolenaar told CBS News. "And if there’s a way to provide more security for the American people through those kinds of discussions, I think it’s important to have it."

Fox News Digital's Greg Norman-Diamond contributed to this report.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at U.S. President Donald Trump’s trip to Asia, European priorities for Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and Houthi territorial gains in Yemen.

On the heels of a disappointing U.S. midterm election for the Republican Party, President Donald Trump departed Washington on Monday for a week of high-stakes meetings with the Indo-Pacific’s biggest powers. From security talks with old allies to historic summits with foreign adversaries, Trump will be reengaging with a region that has largely been relegated to the back burner during his second term.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at U.S. President Donald Trump’s trip to Asia, European priorities for Russia-Ukraine peace talks, and Houthi territorial gains in Yemen.

On the heels of a disappointing U.S. midterm election for the Republican Party, President Donald Trump departed Washington on Monday for a week of high-stakes meetings with the Indo-Pacific’s biggest powers. From security talks with old allies to historic summits with foreign adversaries, Trump will be reengaging with a region that has largely been relegated to the back burner during his second term.

Trump’s trip kicks off in Manila, Philippines, where he will join leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) on Tuesday to discuss some of the greatest threats to the region, including how wars in Iran and Ukraine have impacted the bloc’s economic security. During that time, Trump will also hold in-person talks with his fellow Quadrilateral Security Dialogue leaders—Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi—for the first time since taking office nearly two years ago.

Meeting with the Quad will offer several opportunities for pomp and pageantry; however, experts expect little substance to come out of the summit. “I don’t think the president can hide the fact that he’s not terribly enthusiastic about the gathering,” Kurt Campbell, the co-founder of the Asia Group, a Washington-based geopolitical advisory firm, told FP’s Rishi Iyengar. Instead, the talks will likely serve as a box-checking exercise before Trump can turn his attention to other matters—namely, China.

After less than 24 hours in the Philippines, Trump will head to the Chinese city of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. While there, Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are expected to meet one-on-one with an eye toward maintaining the status quo. That will likely include talks on critical minerals, artificial intelligence, and their recently extended trade truce. Last week’s Nvidia scandal, though, is almost certainly off the table.

The summit’s timing is consequential, as the U.S. midterms reckoning may have shifted Xi’s perception of the Trump administration as it enters its lame-duck period. “Beijing may come to see Trump as a president who remains willing to negotiate on a personal level but is becoming less capable of delivering on major political commitments,” Deng Yuwen argued in Foreign Policy.

Trump, however, may be hoping to challenge that perception with several sideline summits.

On Thursday, he will meet with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin for what China’s Foreign Ministry has called a meeting of “groundbreaking significance.” Although senior administration officials told reporters on Friday that Trump would not bring up the Russia-Ukraine war at the trilateral dialogue, those talks are now expected to discuss the conflict as well as push for denuclearization, though Xi will likely try to rebuff efforts to debate nuclear arms.

Trump has also suggested that he might hold a separate bilateral meeting with Putin, reversing previous assurances from his staff that he had no plans to do so. And he has floated a potential meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during the Shenzhen trip—again, defying past administration claims that talks with Kim were not in the cards.

“We might have Kim Jong Un. He may come. I don’t know—that’s up to President Xi,” Trump told reporters on Monday. Such talks would also likely center on Pyongyang’s nuclear program.

Tuesday, Nov. 17: Xi separately hosts Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori.

Takaichi holds bilateral talks with South Korean President Lee Jae-myung on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit.

European Union defense ministers convene in Brussels.

Israel’s Knesset is set to debate and vote on a new speaker.

Thursday, Nov. 19: The International Court of Justice rules in a case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against the country’s Rohingya Muslims.

Friday, Nov. 20: Takaichi hosts Fujimori.

Brussels hosts the second EU-U.K. leaders’ summit.

Monday, Nov. 23: Polish President Karol Nawrocki begins a five-day trip to Argentina and Chile.

Priority No. 1. The European Union accused Russia on Monday of trying to drag out peace talks while continuing to target Ukraine’s power grid ahead of what is expected to be another harsh winter. “We actually don’t have a cease-fire, and they continue to weaken Ukraine and kill people every single day,” EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas said.

EU leaders also warned against discussing the future of European security with Russia before an immediate truce is reached, stressed that Moscow should be the one to make concessions since Russia began the war, and insisted that EU leaders are prepared to reject any fresh demands from the Kremlin. “We don’t need a new security architecture. We need to restore the one we have,” Kallas said. “Russia has broken all the treaties that underpin it.”

To reiterate that point, the EU imposed new sanctions on Monday targeting nearly 50 Russian financial institutions as well as business executives involved in the energy and oil industries, including Tatyana Kim, the founder of retail giant Wildberries. The bloc also issued fresh asset freezes and travel bans on dozens of people accused of spreading disinformation and pro-Russian propaganda.

The EU’s actions come just days after Putin agreed to allow European representatives to join future Russia-Ukraine peace talks. The EU decided on Friday that its delegation will comprise five major military powers—nonmember Britain as well as France, ‌Germany, Italy, and Poland—and EU institutions.

Military retreat. Saudi Arabia on Monday replaced the commander overseeing its anti-Houthi operations after its Yemeni allies were forced to withdraw from large swaths of Yemen’s Red Sea coast. The retreat marked a significant blow to the Saudi-backed coalition, as the fighters characterized the move—which they described as a redeployment—as necessary to protect the interim capital of Aden.

For months, the Iran-backed Houthis have advanced on the Red Sea and targeted critical energy infrastructure. In October, Yemen’s internationally recognized, Saudi-supported government launched “Dawn of Yemen,” a major counteroffensive aimed at retaking that territory.

But the coalition’s successes have been limited. According to Yemen’s military on Monday, the Houthis ​have now advanced to the southern coastal area of Khor Omairh and are ⁠just 16 miles from government lines at the fishing village of Qawah. That has forced Saudi-backed Yemeni fighters to focus their attention on defending their base of operations in Aden as well as breaking the Houthis’ siege on Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city.

Same-day killings. Separate mass shootings in South Africa over the weekend killed at least 17 people, local police confirmed on Monday. Although the country has struggled to rein in violent crime for years, there has been a recent surge in mass shootings with high fatality rates across the country.

On Sunday, South African authorities found eight bodies in a “bullet-riddled” vehicle outside the city of Pietermaritzburg; efforts to identify the individuals and establish a possible motive remain ongoing. Hours later, police discovered nine people killed by gunshot wounds inside a shack in the informal settlement of Jeffsville, located near the country’s capital. Gauteng Police Commissioner Tommy Mthombeni said that the Jeffsville killings could be related to a shooting at a nearby settlement last year that killed 12 people and injured 13 others, as one of the people killed on Sunday was a “person of interest” in the previous shooting.

The same-day incidents, occurring 330 miles apart, bring the total number of major mass shootings in South Africa to nine since December 2025. Of those, the deadliest was a shooting at a bar in Johannesburg in September that killed 18 people; that killing was one of three mass casualty shootings in the span of a week. South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates in the world.

Fun for the British royal family isn’t just polo matches and chauffeur-driven motorcades. On Monday, Prince William and Princess Catherine kicked off their three-day trip to India with a game of gully cricket in the city of Mumbai. After fielding balls with local children and retired cricketer Sachin Tendulkar, the couple took a ride on the city’s metro rail system to promote the two countries’ close economic ties. This was their first joint visit to India in roughly a decade, and it was the princess’s most high-profile overseas trip since undergoing cancer treatment in 2024.
