Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

In February, Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa’s right-wing coalition ushered in the most sweeping reform to the country’s mining rules in nearly two decades. The government tapped the military to protect strategic mining areas, extended mining contracts from 25 years to as long as 40 years, and replaced its rigorous environmental licensing system with an authorization process that allows projects deemed low impact to skip environmental review and citizen consultation.

Noboa argued that mining is Ecuador’s ticket out of poverty. The country is home to an estimated $220 billion of untapped mineral wealth—mostly gold, copper, and silver, according to the World Bank. But Ecuador has geochemically mapped just 30 percent of its territory, compared to 77 and 85 percent in neighboring Peru and Colombia, respectively. Ecuador’s two existing industrial mines didn’t begin large-scale extraction until 2019.

In February, Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa’s right-wing coalition ushered in the most sweeping reform to the country’s mining rules in nearly two decades. The government tapped the military to protect strategic mining areas, extended mining contracts from 25 years to as long as 40 years, and replaced its rigorous environmental licensing system with an authorization process that allows projects deemed low impact to skip environmental review and citizen consultation.

Noboa argued that mining is Ecuador’s ticket out of poverty. The country is home to an estimated $220 billion of untapped mineral wealth—mostly gold, copper, and silver, according to the World Bank. But Ecuador has geochemically mapped just 30 percent of its territory, compared to 77 and 85 percent in neighboring Peru and Colombia, respectively. Ecuador’s two existing industrial mines didn’t begin large-scale extraction until 2019.

That is partly due to legal protections: Ecuador enshrined the rights of nature in its 2008 constitution, which requires environmental consultations and consent from affected Indigenous groups before major mining projects can begin. The constitution also allows communities to force referendums that can halt extractive projects.

Noboa wants to change that. His government has framed rolling back regulations and militarizing the sector as the path to dismantling illegal mining and bringing sustainable investment to Ecuador. Economists and security experts doubt that his policies can deliver on either front.

“There are potentially massive benefits to [mining]. But there are massive costs, too,” said Monica DeBolle, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics. If your objective is to have the benefits outweigh the costs, she said, “it all boils down to governance.” That has been a major issue for Noboa, who observers have accused of executive overreach.

Noboa was elected president in 2023. He kicked off his pro-mining agenda the next year, attending the world’s largest mining convention in Canada and leading a delegation that secured investment commitments in Ecuador worth nearly $5 billion from companies in Australia, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

After the visit, Noboa used an executive decree to concentrate mining, environmental, security, and financial powers into a single presidential committee. He followed up in 2025 by reopening Ecuador’s mining registry for the first time in seven years and absorbing the Environment Ministry into the Energy and Mining Ministry.

That October, Noboa signed another presidential decree, this time barring nonprofits from “obstruction or interfering” with legally authorized mining projects and requiring them to seek ministry approval for any social programs. He ended the year with yet another decree, handing Ecuador’s mining regulator broad control over concessions and royalties, making it easier for mining companies to move into new areas.

The last decree laid the groundwork for the February overhaul: a sweeping mining reform that loosened environmental licensing, authorized military control of private concessions, and set the stage for a U.S.-backed crackdown on illegal mining. Throughout his time in office, Noboa has also invoked his fight against organized crime to declare states of emergency that curb civil liberties and expand military control over mining provinces.

“No other government—including my own—has ever pushed mining so aggressively,” said Fernando Benalcázar, Ecuador’s former vice minister of mines, who was in office when Ecuador’s two existing large-scale mines—Fruta del Norte and Mirador—came online. Both are in the Amazon rainforest, near the border with Peru. Under Noboa, another six major projects are in various stages of development.

Ecuador’s mining sector generated a total of nearly 12,000 direct jobs through the fourth quarter of 2025, and some estimates project that the industry may create another 460,000 direct and indirect positions by 2030. Minerals, which produced a record $4.16 billion in export revenues in 2025, now fall just behind Ecuador’s other top non-oil exports: cacao, bananas, and shrimp.

But Noboa’s determination to rewrite Ecuador’s mining landscape has put him on a collision course with the constitutional order. The political opposition has argued that Noboa’s policies have relied on sidelining regulatory institutions and local communities. In the words of legislator Verónica Iñiguez, the president’s agenda “put the rat in charge of guarding the cheese.”

Noboa’s mining decrees have not yet faced direct judicial challenges, but Ecuador’s top court has curbed many of his emergency declarations. It has also agreed to hear a challenge to the February mining law brought by Indigenous and community organizations. The plaintiffs argue that the government violated the constitution by failing to consult Indigenous communities, authorizing military activity in ancestral territories, and weakening environmental safeguards.

Although they might promote investment in the short term, aggressive tactics like Noboa’s can backfire in the long term, according to analysts. When top-down mining policy meets resistance in the form of legal setbacks and popular opposition, it creates uncertainty that spooks investors.

“If there’s one thing that investors hate, that one thing is uncertainty,” DeBolle said. “[Policies] at loggerheads with the country’s constitution—that’s a recipe for uncertainty.” The World Bank likewise emphasizes that strong, transparent, and independent government institutions are critical for resource-rich countries to capture and sustain the benefits of mining.

Mounting opposition has already forced Noboa’s government to backtrack on projects that it rushed through. In 2025, the government issued a license for Dundee Precious Metals’ Loma Larga gold-silver-copper mine, despite local resistance and environmental concerns. The site rests atop a fragile ecosystem and a crucial water source, and communities repeatedly voted against mining there. After the rushed approval, local authorities and residents mobilized—filing lawsuits, launching media campaigns, and organizing a “March for Water” with more than 100,000 participants.

Noboa’s office announced in late September that it would revoke the mine’s license. The environmental ministry did so a week later.

Noboa’s push to fast-track mining permissions isn’t just a bid for investment. Paired with military operations against illegal mines, the government also casts approved mining projects as a security tool to weaken organized crime groups, which have pushed into the illegal mining sector over the past decade. By 2024, illegal mining was estimated to generate up to $1 billion a year for criminal groups in Ecuador.

In March, Noboa announced that Ecuador and the United States would increase their cooperation to fight illegal mining and drug trafficking. By October, Ecuador’s military said that it had destroyed more than 1,000 illegal mining camps so far this year. Authorities have not released official casualty figures, but according to local reporting, there have been at least three deaths and many more injuries in these operations.

Luis Córdova Alarcón, who heads a program on conflict and violence at the Central University of Ecuador, said that the logic at the heart of Noboa’s policy is backward. “Legal mining isn’t the opposite of illegal mining. It is its partner in crime,” he said.

Córdova, who described the militarized approach as a “smokescreen,” pointed to illegal extraction within legally granted mining concessions, including arrangements in which concession holders rent access to illegal miners. He also highlighted the formal sector’s role in laundering illegal gold and the  direct involvement of corrupt figures in the criminal economy. His conclusions are backed by the United Nations Office of Drugs and Crime (UNODC), which recently published a report concluding that legally registered corporations can “become involved in illegal mining in different ways,” including infiltration by organized crime groups.

Multinational companies bring their own risks, including corruption, tax evasion, weak ownership transparency, and community conflict, said Julia Yansura, the program director for environmental crime and illicit finance at the FACT Coalition, a Washington-based financial-transparency advocacy group. “I think some governments can’t accept or don’t see risk with these big mining companies. It’s like they’re totally blind to it,” she said.

Easing regulation may open the door to more opaque foreign companies and weaker safeguards, according to Yansura. Militarized crackdowns ignore this sort of illegal mining, targeting small-scale and informal operations tied to organized crime. Yet even when it comes to informal small-scale mining, research has shown militarized approaches to be ineffective in the long run.

Authorities “blow up machinery, harass local people, and then leave,” Yansura said. “That doesn’t actually solve the problem.” In fact, such operations can push miners deeper into illegality, undermine trust in public authorities, and fuel conflict and corruption.

For governments to curb illegal mining and undermine organized crime, UNODC recommends increasing regulation rather than relaxing it, holding big corporations criminally responsible for participating in or facilitating illegal mining activity, and empowering affected communities through democratic engagement.

Noboa is failing on that last front. His mining policies are part of a broader centralization of power that has weakened Ecuador’s democracy. Under the guise of combating illegal mining, Noboa’s administration has pushed through legislation that expands his emergency powers, reduces restrictions on using lethal force against civilians, increases state surveillance, centralizes executive control over protected areas, and targets financing for environmental nongovernmental organization.

Indigenous groups, human rights advocates, and environmental defenders say that Noboa’s administration has used these laws to go after individuals who oppose his mining policies. They point to recent criminal charges against water defenders, the violent police dispersal of anti-mining protests in the capital of Quito in February, and the conviction of at least 15 anti-mining protesters on criminal charges throughout the course of this year.

“Quite simply, what the Ecuadorian government is doing is rolling back rights and eroding the institutions meant to protect them,” Iñiguez said.

In August 2025, when Ecuador’s highest court challenged the constitutionality of some of the new laws, Noboa led a march on the court, and senior members of his administration called judges “enemies of the citizenry,” alarming observers. He defended the suspended security measures and his efforts to pressure Ecuadorian institutions as necessary to combat criminal gangs, telling a crowd at the march that “[w]e are here to pursue justice and peace.”

A month later, when Ecuador’s powerful Indigenous movement CONAIE declared a nationwide strike triggered by the end of fuel subsidies, Noboa deployed the military to break up roadblocks, resulting in at least three civilian deaths, and vowed to prosecute protest leaders for terrorism under a new statute. In October 2025, CONAIE called off the strike, citing fear of government violence.

Noboa’s aggressive approach initially appeared popular with a public preoccupied with crime. But that changed on Nov. 16, 2025, when Ecuadorians went to the polls to vote in a national referendum. In a surprise upset, Noboa lost all four questions that would have further concentrated power in the executive. The biggest rebuke was to his proposal to convene a constituent assembly: Voters rejected rewriting Ecuador’s environmentally protective constitution.

Continuing to push through mining policy at odds with Ecuador’s constitution may turn out to be Noboa’s Achilles heel. Polling showed a sharp decline in the president’s approval ratings in the first half of this year compared to 2025. “The decline stems directly from his failure to respect the mandate of the ballot box,” Iñiguez said.

Anastasia Austin is an award-winning investigative journalist covering politics, economics, environmental issues, and organized crime in Latin America. X: @nastia492

#5858. Trump's $50B air traffic control overhaul faces GOP pushback after nationwide ground stop

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy calls on Congress to invest in aviation software and infrastructure upgrades following a nationwide FAA ground stop on 'Hannity.'

The Trump administration is pressing Congress for tens of billions in emergency funding to upgrade the nation’s air traffic control systems, but even Senate Republicans are reluctant to pay the bill.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and President Donald Trump called on lawmakers to shell out $50 billion in funding after a ground stop on Friday caused thousands of flight cancellations and blamed Congress for not doling out money previously to upgrade aging air traffic control communications infrastructure.

But Congress did send $12.5 billion to the Department of Transportation as part of the "big, beautiful bill" last year meant to upgrade the archaic systems, and Republicans want receipts on what happened to the money.

FAA SAYS AIR TRAVEL SHOULD BE BACK TO NORMAL SUNDAY AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP

Secretary Sean Duffy speaks during a press briefing at Department of Transportation headquarters on Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington, D.C. The briefing followed a nationwide communications outage that grounded flights across the United States the previous day. (Aaron Schwartz/AFP via Getty Images)

"Only about four [billion] has been spent," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said. "There was about eight billion of that still sitting around."

Duffy is slated to meet with Senate Republicans behind closed doors on Tuesday where lawmakers expect a full breakdown of what happened and where the money has gone and why, suddenly, the administration is seeking an additional $20 billion.

"I haven't seen how they're gonna use it. I mean, in my business, you know, I spent a lot of money, and I built companies," Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital. "And I understood what I was going to spend it on before I ever did anything. I'd have a budget and what the timeline is, who's gonna do it, all that stuff."

FORMER TOP FAA OFFICIAL WARNS OF 48-HOUR RECOVERY AFTER AGING TECH 'OVERWHELMED' AHEAD OF GROUND STOP

Data from the Department of Transportation (DOT) obtained by Fox News Digital showed that roughly $3.7 billion had been spent on a variety of projects, while the remainder is tied to contracts, unspent or planned for near-term upgrades, like facility consolidation.

Thune declined to say whether he had confidence in Duffy’s handling of the situation and noted that the administration had already made a separate ask for $30 billion, a chunk of which was meant to continue upgrades to air traffic control.

"I mean, there's some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is," Thune said. "But I think we have attempted to do everything we can to ensure that the concerns they have about modernization are being met."

Duffy’s explanation of the ground stop was attributed to replacing copper wiring in communications equipment with fiber-optic cable. About $4.8 billion of the initial funding pot was for copper wire replacement, of which about $2.3 billion has been spent, which translates to roughly 70% completion of the telecommunications replacement program, according to the DOT.

4 CRITICAL TRAVEL ISSUES FOR THOSE DELAYED AND DISRUPTED BY FAA NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., argued that Democrats were continuing their push to keep DHS closed because it was "politically advantageous." (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

A DOT spokesperson told Fox News Digital that the "Department has made clear for the last two years — separate funding is needed" for other work because DOT "does not have the legal flexibility to move funds from one workstream to another."

"He needs to talk to me like I'm a reasonably intelligent 10th grader," Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said. "The American people are not experts on telecommunications … nor am I."

Kennedy, who is a member of the Transportation, Housing and Urban Development Appropriations Subcommittee, which controls the DOT's purse strings, said he was more than "willing to appropriate money to fix this," but needed to understand the problem first.

"I mean, we had an outage today, some problems with a number of our banks," Kennedy said. "There have been some problems in Europe with the Internet controlling temperatures of grocery stores. I mean, this is happening a lot. I'm not saying there's a connection, but if there is, they need to tell us."

Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., told Fox News Digital that the initial $12.5 billion was "a starting point — it wasn’t everything."

"We've seen nothing yet of what's the rest of the request," Lankford said. "So that does seem like, ‘Hey, grab a number out of the air. It needs to be big.’"

Lankford added that Duffy needed to give a "postmortem" on what happened, and that whatever the administration is asking for in upgrades needs to be "shovel-ready."

"This is a zero fail operation," he said. "He's keenly aware of that."

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

#5857. Democrats Shouldn’t Squander Their Chance to Launch a Foreign Policy Revolution

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

MATTHEW DUSS is Executive Vice President of the Center for International Policy. From 2017 to 2022, he served as Chief Foreign Policy Adviser to Senator Bernie Sanders.

The Imperative of Ambition in a New Congress

Tuesday’s election made clear that endless wars, political corruption, and the high cost of living are three of the American public’s top concerns. They are deeply interrelated—and the new Congress must address all three. That will require a true foreign policy revolution that grapples not just with the outrages and failures of the Trump administration’s foreign policy but also with the ways in which past Democratic or Democrat-supported foreign policies have contributed to today’s crisis. There will be a temptation among some Democratic leaders, in Congress and beyond, to limit the scope or pace of change. But to find a way out of today’s crisis and move beyond the failures that have afflicted American foreign policy for the past several decades, Democrats will need to have the courage to face a hard truth: that President Donald Trump’s abuses of power and unilateral warmaking are not so much a break from Washington’s militarist mindset as they are a particularly aggressive, predatory expression of it.

The incoming Democratic majority will face a national security environment in which the most severe challenges to U.S. safety and prosperity come from within. That’s why Congress should shut down the Iran war immediately but also recognize that it can make the United States more secure only if it pairs a foreign policy shift with a frontal assault on spiraling costs and political corruption. Political polarization; government corruption and dysfunction; increasing dominance of political and economic life by a small handful of mercurial oligarchs; and a president who recklessly and unilaterally launches unauthorized military interventions while relentlessly seeking opportunities to enrich himself, his family, and his cronies—all pose more immediate danger to the safety and prosperity of the American people than does any foreign enemy.

When Democrats take control of Congress in January, they will have considerable power to challenge the corruption and malfeasance of the Trump administration. Control of committees and of the congressional calendar will provide the opportunity for sorely needed oversight. But although the Trump administration deserves aggressive investigation, Democrats must aim higher—and use the opportunity to articulate a genuinely compelling alternative for American foreign policy.

The first and most urgent task will be ending the Iran war, a reckless and unpopular conflict that has become even less popular as Americans have felt its effects on their wallets. Congress must respond to widespread bipartisan anger among voters at Trump’s war and abuse of war powers by using all the tools it has, especially its power to cut funding. It has been encouraging to see Democrats continuing to oppose any supplemental budget request by the administration for the war. It is an area where Democrats have gotten tripped up in the past when they’ve been afraid of accusations that they don’t “support the troops” if they oppose funding for foolish, counterproductive wars. With Democrats having held firm against any additional funding for the war, those days appear to be gone. That is good.

But Democrats need to go further. They should be prepared to oppose all funding for the military, including blocking votes on the National Defense Authorization Act, the annual bill setting out the broad scope and budget for the Defense Department, in order to put an end to hostilities in Iran. In fact, not only should they be willing to withhold funding from the Pentagon, but they should also be willing to withhold funding for the entire government, and threaten another government shutdown if the bill does not prohibit any funding for Trump’s war. December 11 is the deadline for a continuing resolution to keep the government funded and operating. If ever there was a reason for Democrats to threaten to withhold their votes, stopping a blatantly illegal and globally destructive war that American voters have now resoundingly rebuked is it.

Democrats must also be willing to take a hard look at the continuity between Trump’s use of military violence and past uses of force by administrations of both parties, and the bipartisan support for that violence. The groundwork for the Iran war was laid by the Biden administration’s unstinting support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza (as even some former administration officials have acknowledged), but also by years of U.S. refusal to impose any consequences on the Israeli government despite clear evidence of ongoing violations of human rights and international law. Trump’s strikes on alleged “narcoterrorist” drug boats in the Caribbean represent the logical evolution of long-standing treatment of the United States’ drug problem as a “war,” and of casually applying the label of “terrorist” to justify any and all measures, including execution without due process. Seeking accountability for these abuses will require acknowledging the past complicity of both Republicans and Democrats.

Democrats must also take on corruption, a key node connecting the country’s domestic and foreign policy crises. In doing so, they will be walking through an open door. Polls consistently show that political corruption is high on Americans’ list of concerns. According to a recent Harris poll conducted for The Guardian, “Nearly nine out of 10 Americans said that government corruption, as defined as elected officials putting their own or their donors’ financial interests ahead of the public’s, is a problem.” A mid-October CNBC All-America Economic Survey found that voters are more concerned about government corruption than any other issue, including high grocery and gas prices. In September, Gallup reported that “Americans’ perceptions of government corruption in the U.S. are at their highest level in 20 years, with 89% of U.S. adults saying it is widespread.”

To say that the Trump administration provides a target-rich environment for a strong anticorruption push is to commit felony understatement. Exposing foreign gifts to Trump and conflicts of interest by family members, contracts awarded to Trump’s oligarch donors and new tech buddies, and the selling of pardons, as well as restoring enforcement of the Corporate Transparency Act, the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, and related task forces, should all be part of the plan. Democrats should drill down into Trump’s wildly corrupt “Board of Peace” for Gaza, which U.S. Representative Jamie Raskin, the Maryland Democrat set to chair the House Judiciary Committee, rightly referred to as a “global slush fund.” The obvious conflicts of interests of Trump’s diplomatic envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner also demand investigation.

The good news is that effective anticorruption does not necessarily require new legislation; it merely requires that existing legislation be enforced. An August 2025 essay in Foreign Affairs, co-authored with my colleagues Casey Michel and Trevor Sutton, laid out a more expansive case for Democrats putting anticorruption at the center of their foreign policy platform. (A recent essay by Casey Michel lays out a more detailed agenda for the new Congress.)

Ultimately, the most important step toward tackling corruption will be reforming the campaign finance system. The United States is an outlier among developed democracies in that its system of campaign finance allows for what is essentially legalized bribery. Legislators speak openly about campaign contributors expecting “returns on investment” for their political donations. This is an outrage. In recent years, foreign actors have increasingly begun bankrolling American legislators, taking advantage of massive loopholes in campaign finance laws and the Federal Election Commission’s lack of enforcement.

Confronting this will be no small task. At a minimum, Congress must move to legislate a response to the Supreme Court’s 2010 Citizens United decision, which effectively greenlighted bottomless campaign funding from American corporations. It must also reform the Federal Election Commission, providing the body with much-needed resources to investigate campaign finance crimes and restoring the practice of allowing congressional appointments to the commission, which has become little more than an appendage of the executive branch.

All of the above steps must be connected to the top concern among American voters at this moment—the high cost of living. Democrats have disagreements in several policy areas, particularly in foreign policy. Their coalition is diverse. But there is consensus around addressing Americans’ material needs urgently and aggressively. Such an approach would confront Trump’s reckless use of tariffs (while recognizing that the neoliberal taboo on tariffs is a thing of the past), rising gas prices because of the Iran war, the need to restore the global minimum tax, the threat of job losses to AI, and the increased power of tech oligarchs over Americans’ economic and political lives, including on foreign policy, as Elon Musk’s restriction of Ukraine’s Starlink connection demonstrated. The approach should involve a mix of tactics, including hearings, oversight investigations, and legislative proposals.

Many of these efforts may not produce new laws in the next two years. But they could become the backbone of a winning agenda for Congress and for a Democratic administration in 2029. Most important, they would represent a step toward the forging of a new American political consensus on which a new and durable foreign policy can be built.

How Far Will He Go to Make Peace—and War?

#5855. Will Iraqi Kurdistan Break Apart?

Analysis: Will Iraqi Kurdistan Break Apart?

An escalating confrontation between the two constituent parts of Iraqi Kurdistan is threatening to tear the besieged region apart. Since 2006, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) and the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), which fought a brutal civil war in the 1990s, have formed an uneasy alliance to govern the predominantly-Kurdish, autonomous region of northern Iraq. So far, the region and the alliance have survived a war with the Islamic State in 2014 and more than 1,000 attacks by Iran and its proxies since the start of 2026.

Now, however, a fight over the allotment of parliamentary seats and cabinet positions is pushing both parties toward a formal split. On Thursday, Nov. 5, the PUK formally withdrew from the region’s joint government. If the division worsens, it could damage the Iraqi Kurdistan's hard-won autonomy, threaten international support, and create new difficulties for citizens in their everyday lives.

An escalating confrontation between the two constituent parts of Iraqi Kurdistan is threatening to tear the besieged region apart. Since 2006, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) and the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), which fought a brutal civil war in the 1990s, have formed an uneasy alliance to govern the predominantly-Kurdish, autonomous region of northern Iraq. So far, the region and the alliance have survived a war with the Islamic State in 2014 and more than 1,000 attacks by Iran and its proxies since the start of 2026.

Now, however, a fight over the allotment of parliamentary seats and cabinet positions is pushing both parties toward a formal split. On Thursday, Nov. 5, the PUK formally withdrew from the region’s joint government. If the division worsens, it could damage the Iraqi Kurdistan’s hard-won autonomy, threaten international support, and create new difficulties for citizens in their everyday lives.

On Nov. 11, U.S. Ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack told the Kurdish parties that the Trump administration’s advice was to “get over it.” Barrack also spoke to Kurdish officials from both the PUK and KDP that week and underlined the importance of a united Kurdistan Region. In response, Bafel Talabani, the head of the PUK, called on the KDP to “get over it.” In the coming weeks, the parties’ willingness to compromise will determine if they can overcome their differences and prevent the breakup of the autonomous region.

Under U.S. mediation, the KDP and the PUK reached an agreement in 2006 whereby the KDP would control the presidency in Kurdistan and the PUK would control the Iraqi presidency in Baghdad. But this strategic agreement came under pressure after the PUK started to lose parliamentary seats to smaller opposition parties in 2009. In 2013, the KDP won 38 seats out of 100 in the Kurdish parliament compared to only 18 for the PUK. Then, in 2018, the KDP also attempted to challenge the PUK’s hold on the Iraqi presidency.

At the same time, the PUK also faced an internal power struggle after the death of its leader, Jalal Talabani, in 2017. Eventually, Talabani’s son Bafel Talabani took over the party in 2022, while his rival and cousin, Lahur Talabani, was subsequently given a five-year prison sentence for allegedly plotting an assassination, which he denies.

After elections in October 2024, the KDP again emerged as the largest party with 39 seats, as compared to 23 for the PUK. The KDP went on to argue that the allotment of cabinet roles and other government positions should reflect the parties’ respective seat shares, while the PUK maintained that they should be divided on a 50-50 basis, as stipulated in the 2006 agreement.

As a result of this disagreement, the Kurdistan Region has been without a functioning parliament since late 2024. On Nov. 4, however, the KDP managed to reach the legal quorum of 51 seats in order to convene the Kurdistan Region’s parliament. Having secured this majority with the help of defectors from opposition parties and three PUK members, the KDP proceeded to elect a new Presidency Board.

Hoshyar Siwaily, the head of the KDP’s foreign relations office, told Foreign Policy that over the past two years, the KDP and PUK have held intensive negotiations on forming a new government. However, he said that the negotiations between the two parties over the allocation of ministerial and senior government positions remained inconclusive, bringing the process to an impasse.

“The KDP was therefore compelled to form a parliamentary majority and reactivate the Kurdistan Parliament,” Siwaily said.

Saadi Ahmed Pira, a member of the PUK’s political bureau, disputed this assessment, claiming that while negotiations were still underway, and the deadlock was close to being solved, the KDP unilaterally decided to call for a session of parliament.

“The KDP was able to get the required number of MPs to meet the required 50+1 quorum by means of compensating several of our MPs and some MPs from other parties with large amounts of money, in essence bribing them to buy their votes,” Pira said.

The KDP denied the PUK’s allegations. “Almost all members of the other parties who attended the session categorically denied any wrongdoing, including allegations that they had received financial favors from the KDP,” Siwaily said.

In response to these developments, PUK leader Bafel Talabani said he was pulling out of the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) administration and threatened to form his own government outside of the KRG if the KDP moved ahead with its new parliamentary majority.

“You appoint a president of the region, we will appoint a president of the region. You appoint ministers, we will appoint ministers,” Talabani stated.

The KDP claims that it will do “everything in its power to prevent such a disastrous outcome.” On Nov. 9, KDP President Masoud Barzani called on the PUK to sit down with the KDP to end the political crisis in the region. So far, Talabani has publicly dismissed the statement as “not serious.”

Both parties will now look to Baghdad for support. On Nov. 9, KRG Prime Minister Masrour Barzani, a leader within the KDP, met with the Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi. After his visit, Barzani stated that Baghdad had agreed to continue paying all salaries in the region through the KRG administration. Bafel Talabani also traveled to Baghdad on Nov. 12 to lobby for his party and met with Iraqi leaders, including Iranian-backed Iraqi factions.

The PUK filed a lawsuit in Iraq’s top court in Baghdad on Nov. 10 to annul the reactivation of the parliament. On Nov. 15, the court rejected a separate request to suspend the parliament, and it will have a hearing on Dec. 14 on whether to reduce the KRG’s powers to a caretaker government.

Mohammed A. Salih, a nonresident senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, told Foreign Policy that neither side wants to preclude reconciliation. “Both have shown considerable flexibility and pragmatism by keeping the door open for further negotiations and a negotiated settlement,” he said, adding, “The PUK’s withdrawal of its ministers from the cabinet is a blow to the KRG, but it will not bring the government down.”

Salih argued that a lasting break would run counter U.S. strategic interests in Iraq, particularly given ongoing concerns over Iranian influence. “Messaging from the U.S. side also suggests that Washington does not want to see the Kurdistan Region divided into two separate administrations,” he said.

If divisions persist, the price will also be paid by normal citizens. Binar Faeq Karim, an affiliate researcher at the think tank London Dialogue, suggested residents of the region would face “more complicated governance, difficulties in coordinating public services and economic policy and greater uncertainty over salaries, revenues and relations with Baghdad.”

Former U.S. Ambassador to Croatia Peter Galbraith, who has had a close relationship with the Kurds for more than four decades, told Foreign Policy that “recreating two administrations, as existed in the 1990s, would undermine all that has been achieved [by the Kurds] to date.”

“I understand bitter partisan differences—they exist in the U.S. as well—but it is sad when politicians allow them to threaten the very existence of Kurdistan,” Galbraith said.

Wladimir van Wilgenburg is an analyst and journalist specializing in Kurdish affairs who has co-authored two books focusing on the Kurds in Syria. X: @vvanwilgenburg

#5854. Connecticut solar projects directly support Veterans Affairs campus

The Connecticut Department of Veterans Affairs (DVA), Connecticut Green Bank and their partners recently marked the completion of solar installations serving DVA’s main campus and skilled nursing facility in Rocky Hill, Connecticut.

The projects will deliver renewable electricity and reduce energy costs at the campus. The Green Bank developed the projects through its Solar Marketplace Assistance Program Plus (Solar MkAP+). Kearsarge Energy has partnered with Connecticut Green Bank as the long-term owners of these projects as well as nine others and will also oversee operations and maintenance. Greenskies Clean Energy was the engineering, procurement and construction contractor for the two DVA installations.

“To Gov. Lamont and your administration, thank you for having the vision for the GreenerGov CT initiative, providing reliable, environmentally friendly and cost-saving energy for residents and businesses in Connecticut, which is one of your top priorities, along with countless others, enabling Connecticut’s 3.6 million residents to thrive,” said Ron Welch, a retired brigadier general with the U.S. Army, and commissioner of the DVA. “Our team at the Connecticut Department of Veterans Affairs thanks you for your full support of this solar field project and for all you do through your significant partnerships to sustain and improve the environment and the quality of life for Connecticut residents and beyond.”

The two systems have a combined capacity of 1.404 MWDC and are projected to generate approximately 1.84 million kWh of electricity annually. The systems are projected to offset 85% of electricity use for the skilled nursing facility and 35% of the electricity use at the main campus building.

“This project brings together two important commitments: advancing sustainability in state government and supporting the people who have served our nation,” said Michelle Gilman, commissioner of the Department of Administrative Services. “DAS is proud to support this project and the broader Greener Gov CT partnership.”

The two arrays built at the Rocky Hill campus are 604.8 kWDC and 799.2 kWDC.

#5853. Trump Treasury aims to slam shut banking loopholes that could enable fraud tied to illegal immigration

Federal law enforcement agencies execute 17 search warrants in Minnesota to dismantle an alleged massive, multi-million-dollar fraud scheme targeting vulnerable public programs. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, FBI Director Kash Patel and CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz announce the coordinated federal crackdown during a joint press conference. Bessent confirms that the Internal Revenue Service is actively assisting with the investigations.

FIRST ON FOX: The Trump administration is moving to tighten financial safeguards it says could help stop illegal immigrants from exploiting the U.S. banking system, putting banks on notice to scrutinize business ownership more closely when warning signs emerge.

The proposed rule from the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) is part of President Donald Trump’s effort to address what his administration calls national security and public safety risks tied to illicit financial activity and people in the country illegally.

In short, the proposal would give banks more leeway to dig into who owns a business when they see potential red flags.

APPEALS COURT UPHOLDS ORDER BLOCKING IRS FROM SHARING TAXPAYER DATA WITH ICE

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the proposed rule would give financial institutions more flexibility to assess risk and strengthen efforts to combat financial crime. (Reuters)

Trump’s executive order directs Treasury to strengthen customer due diligence. It says financial institutions should be able to seek information about immigration status and work authorization when relevant to assessing fraud or other illicit activity.

Under the proposal, covered institutions could obtain additional information about the beneficial owners of business customers to mitigate risk or address supervisory concerns. The rule would also end the requirement to reverify those owners each time an existing customer opens a new account and spell out what information banks must collect.

TRUMP ADMIN’S FRAUD CRACKDOWN TARGETS FOREIGNERS ACCUSED OF INFILTRATING US FEDERAL PROGRAMS

President Donald Trump directed Treasury to strengthen customer due diligence at financial institutions, with the administration citing concerns about illicit finance and risks tied to people in the country illegally. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

The proposal does not require banks to verify every customer’s immigration status. FinCEN says the changes are intended to combat money laundering and terrorist financing while cutting unnecessary compliance burdens.

"Financial institutions are on the front lines of protecting our financial systems from criminal organizations and cartels that target law-abiding businesses and workers," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.

He said the proposal would give institutions more flexibility to combat risk and strengthen the fight against financial crime.

An anti-ICE sign in the window of a gas station in Minneapolis, Minn., January 8, 2026. (Preston Mizell/Fox News Digital)

FinCEN is accepting public comments for 60 days after the proposal is published in the Federal Register.

Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

#5851. 5 Freshmen Democratic Lawmakers to Watch

In January, dozens of new Democratic lawmakers will enter the House of Representatives—many with strong U.S. foreign-policy and national security views.

And while they won’t have the seniority to chair major committees, they could still prove incredibly influential. Just look at the lawmakers who swept in during the last Democratic wave election in 2018 and went on to become household names—figures such as Ilhan Omar, Rashida Tlaib, and Deb Haaland. Some have gone on to win governorships and Senate seats. One—Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez—is even widely speculated to be considering a high-profile run at the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination.

In January, dozens of new Democratic lawmakers will enter the House of Representatives—many with strong U.S. foreign-policy and national security views.

And while they won’t have the seniority to chair major committees, they could still prove incredibly influential. Just look at the lawmakers who swept in during the last Democratic wave election in 2018 and went on to become household names—figures such as Ilhan Omar, Rashida Tlaib, and Deb Haaland. Some have gone on to win governorships and Senate seats. One—Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez—is even widely speculated to be considering a high-profile run at the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination.

Here are five incoming House Democrats who could end up being just as formidable presences in the next Congress, especially on foreign policy and national security.

Retired Army Lt. Col. Fred Wellman rode the blue tsunami to topple a longtime Republican lawmaker. His background as a helicopter pilot with multiple combat tours followed by work in political communications and veterans’ advocacy could position him to be a thorn in the side of the Trump administration and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Wellman served for 22 years in the Army and saw combat four times, including during the first Gulf War and three tours in Iraq. Formerly a lifelong Republican, Wellman switched parties after becoming disgusted with Donald Trump’s disparagement of former Sen. John McCain’s prisoner-of-war status. He would go on to be a veterans’ affairs advisor and later the executive director of the Lincoln Project, a political action committee that drew national attention in the 2020 presidential contest for its acerbic ads that lampooned Trump’s character and record.

Wellman has been a fierce critic of Trump’s decision to launch a war against Iran without congressional authorization. He supports continued military assistance to Ukraine and the Block the Bombs Act, legislation popular with progressives that would prohibit the export of some of the United States’ most powerful bombs to Israel.

Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral, is another former Republican who flipped a deeply red district. Laubacher narrowly unseated one of MAGA’s most prominent and polarizing House members, Rep. Lauren Boebert, in Colorado’s reddest district.

Laubacher’s distinguished 34-year Navy career, which focused on intelligence matters and South Asia, could propel her to assignments on Capitol Hill’s national security committees, such as House Armed Services or House Intelligence, where her insider knowledge of U.S. surveillance technology and the defense-industrial base bureaucracy is likely to be valued.

In her final years of military service, Laubacher served as defense attaché to India and then on the National Security Council during the Biden administration as the point person for South Asia. During her stint as the top defense official at the U.S. Embassy in New Delhi, Laubacher was credited with playing an important role in facilitating U.S. support for the Indian military during a series of violent 2020 standoffs with the Chinese army along the two countries’ disputed Himalayan border.

Her campaign focused on affordability issues and connecting Trump’s tariff policies and the Iran war to higher cost of living, as well as improving care and services for veterans. She is a member of the Blue Dogs, a caucus of moderate and conservative-leaning House Democrats. Laubacher wants an end to U.S. taxpayer-financed military support for Israel but supports the transfer of weapons to the country on a “case by case basis.”

Democrats feel they have a mandate to put conditions on U.S. support for Israel.

The world has changed. A new approach must take that into account.

It wasn’t just Iran. Israel, tariffs, and immigration also loomed large in voters’ minds.

Also hailing from Colorado but from the opposite wing of the Democratic Party is Melat Kiros, a democratic socialist who at 29 years old will become the youngest female lawmaker in Congress in January. Kiros immigrated as a baby with her family from Ethiopia.

As a junior corporate attorney, she was fired from her job at a prominent law firm for refusing to take down an open letter she published defending law students who expressed pro-Palestinian views in the weeks after Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel. Kiros, who has accused Israel of committing genocide, drew connections to her family’s own experiences, having lost family members to what she called the recent “genocidal war against Tigrayans by the Ethiopian and Eritrean governments.”

This summer, Kiros successfully challenged from the left the 15-term incumbent progressive lawmaker Rep. Diana DeGette to win the Democratic nomination for the solid blue Denver-area congressional seat. She argued that DeGette and other establishment Democrats had been ineffective in combating Trump. During the primary, Kiros made Israel a distinguishing issue between herself and DeGette. She supports an arms embargo to the country that would cover even defensive systems such as the Iron Dome missile shield.

In the House, Kiros is expected to align with other far-left young progressives such as Ocasio-Cortez. Although Kiros received critical primary campaign backing from the Democratic Socialists of America, she has said she does not share the national organization’s position that the United States should withdraw from NATO.

Like Kiros, Brad Lander successfully ran to the left of an establishment Democrat in a deep blue district where support for Israel was a key dividing issue. But Lander’s Jewish faith and victory over a pro-Israel incumbent in one of the most Jewish districts in the United States (New York’s 10th) could make him a potent Capitol Hill foil for the Israeli government.

Lander, a former New York City councilman and comptroller, is a political ally of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. And he has already been mixing it up online and offline with members of both Israel’s political opposition and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right government. Like many other progressive House Democrats, Lander, whose district includes Lower Manhattan and Brooklyn, supports the Block the Bombs Act.

When former Israeli Prime Minister Yair Lapid wrote on X shortly after the U.S. midterm elections that his country’s next government should prioritize repairing ties with moderate Democrats in Congress as well as embark on a public relations tour of the United States, Lander pushed back hard.

“[Y]ou’re not listening to what American voters—Jewish and non-Jewish—are saying,” Lander wrote on X in response. “We aren’t starving for a barnstorming tour. We’re hungry to see respect for international law and human rights.”

Just a few weeks earlier during a solidarity visit to the West Bank to help Palestinian farmers harvest their olive crop, Lander was detained for several hours by the Israeli military, which said it was because his trip presented a “security risk.”

“Yet one more element of escalating, and very clearly state-sponsored ethnic cleansing,” Lander wrote of the experience.

Speaking of potent foils, Hegseth may face one of his own making when he is eventually called to testify before the House oversight committees.

Nancy Lacore is another retired Navy admiral who narrowly flipped a solidly conservative district in the midterms. But Lacore, who won her South Carolina House seat by just over 3,000 votes, is also one of the highest-ranking officers to be ousted by Hegseth. Her 35-year Navy career, including her most recent position as the chief of the Navy Reserve, would seem to make her a strong candidate for membership on the House Armed Services Committee.

Lacore has said she doesn’t know why Hegseth fired her, but she went on to make her opposition to his leadership a central tenet of her campaign. “Pete Hegseth is the most unqualified secretary that this nation has seen,” Lacore said in an interview with CBS News after winning election. “He has caused significant damage to us as a country and put us at risk and really damaged the readiness of our entire military force.”

The retired three-star vice admiral was a registered Republican until 2016, when Trump became the party’s leader. In January, she will become the highest-ranking female military officer ever to serve in Congress.

Rachel Oswald is a staff writer at Foreign Policy. X: @OswaldRachel

#5850. A Recipe for Disaster in Taiwan

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

REBECCA LISSNER is Senior Fellow for U.S. Foreign Policy and Director of the Future of American Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations. She served as Deputy Assistant to the President and Principal Deputy National Security Adviser to the Vice President during the Biden administration.

MIRA RAPP-HOOPER is a Visiting Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution. She was Special Assistant to the President and Senior Director for East Asia and Oceania and Director for Indo-Pacific Strategy at the U.S. National Security Council during the Biden administration.

Just a few years ago, U.S. President Joe Biden caused a stir when he confirmed publicly that his administration would defend Taiwan if the island were attacked by China—a divergence from the traditional U.S. policy of strategic ambiguity, in which Washington does not commit to taking any particular action. In May, U.S. President Donald Trump made waves for taking a different position. In a television interview, he described Taiwan as “a very good negotiating chip” in dealings with Beijing and mused that the island was close to China but far from the United States, implying that U.S. interests in Taiwan were negligible. In doing so, Trump seemed to confirm something many Asia watchers had feared: that this U.S. president would be willing to loosen the United States’ commitment to Taiwan to bolster his relationship with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

A few days later, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee that there had been no change in U.S. policy toward Taiwan. But Trump’s words were alarming nonetheless—in part because they reflect a shift in Washington that goes beyond the Oval Office. Since 2025, politicians from both parties have been shying away from affirming the United States’ long-standing support for Taiwan. Meanwhile, China is developing new strategies to coerce Taiwan without going to war, and Beijing will be increasingly tempted to use them if it judges that the U.S. commitment to Taiwan is waning among both politicians and the public.

Yet that would be a grave miscalculation on China’s part. In fact, the United States’ interests in Taiwan are growing, not diminishing. Whatever the nature of Washington’s rhetoric right now, the United States would have to respond to any action by Beijing that threatened those interests, and both countries would then face a great-power crisis. To defuse this dangerous situation, American leaders must update the United States’ Taiwan strategy to reflect a new reality—and they should begin immediately.

Taiwan’s unique international status has long made U.S. policy complex. The Republic of China, now known as Taiwan, was a World War II ally of the United States. When the People’s Republic of China was founded on the mainland, in 1949, the Republic of China’s president, Chiang Kai-shek, decamped to Taiwan, and the United States maintained formal diplomatic ties with Chiang’s government, not the People’s Republic of China. In 1954, as the Cold War crested in the Pacific, the United States concluded a formal mutual defense treaty with Taiwan, in part to forestall increasingly aggressive artillery barrages from the mainland. Nearly 20 years later, however, when U.S. President Richard Nixon and his national security adviser, Henry Kissinger, began to engineer a diplomatic opening to the government in Beijing, they knew it would cost Taiwan.

In part because they understood that building diplomatic ties with Beijing would be painful for Taiwan and cause controversy in Congress, where Taipei had many boosters, Nixon and Kissinger slow-walked the process. So did Nixon’s successor, President Gerald Ford. It finally fell to President Jimmy Carter to make the change. On January 1, 1979, the United States ended its alliance with Taiwan and recognized the mainland government as “the sole legal Government of China.” Congress was irate. Lawmakers from both parties quickly drafted the 1979 Taiwan Relations Act, which remains in force. The law requires Washington to provide Taipei with defensive arms, creating the trappings of an alliance with Taiwan despite the relationship’s unofficial status. In 1982, the Reagan administration made an additional set of commitments to Taiwan, known as the Six Assurances. These include an affirmation that Washington does not endorse Beijing’s sovereignty claims over Taiwan and a promise that the United States would not use arms sales to Taiwan as a bargaining chip.

In the 50 years since, U.S. Taiwan policy has been remarkably successful. Through its partnership and arms sales, the United States has helped underwrite peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait, and Taiwan has thrived as a democracy and an economy, even as Washington has maintained a relationship with Beijing. But U.S. commitments to Taiwan have lately come under increasing strain. China has proceeded with a massive military buildup designed to give Beijing the option to take Taiwan by force; used coercive economic tactics, launched cyberattacks, and interfered in elections to put pressure on Taipei; and run frequent army and coast guard exercises to demonstrate its ability to strangle the island. All of this has stoked concerns across the Pacific that the United States’ long-standing partnership might not be enough to keep the peace in the Taiwan Strait.

The fear that China could attempt to retake Taiwan by force, possibly during Xi’s tenure, has grown in recent years. Analysts have frequently cited 2027 as the beginning of the window of maximum danger, based on a 2021 statement made by Philip Davidson, the former commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, about when the People’s Liberation Army might be prepared for an invasion. But this timeline was never hard and fast, and Xi’s recent purge of more than 100 officers has likely delayed the military’s readiness. U.S. intelligence assessments do not anticipate an invasion of Taiwan next year, and most scholars believe the Chinese government would consider such a move as a last resort only if unification could not be accomplished by other means.

The primary danger now is that Xi will escalate a pressure campaign designed to coerce Taiwan into negotiating a change in its status. Since 2025, China’s leaders have used their diplomatic channels to the Trump administration, including Xi’s direct line to Trump, to insist on American concessions on Taiwan in exchange for progress in trade talks. In May, China secured a pause on a planned $14 billion U.S. arms sale and other defense funding for Taiwan. Beijing may hope that additional incremental moves will further weaken Taiwanese confidence in the United States and that such actions will be difficult for Trump or a future U.S. president to reverse.

China is also clearly planning for more dramatic forms of coercion. It has a few options: since 2022, China’s military has practiced blockades of Taiwan, and its coast guard has simulated a quarantine of the island’s major ports. Beijing could also use customs enforcement or other administrative measures to attempt to assert its jurisdiction over Taiwan while minimizing the likelihood that the United States would intervene to stop it. If Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, who favors Taiwanese independence but has not pursued it in office, is reelected in 2028 and Chinese leaders believe that the path to a peaceful unification is closing, Xi may consider using these tools against the island in late 2028 or early 2029, before a new U.S. administration takes office. Given Trump’s alienation of U.S. allies in Asia and Europe and Washington’s limited means to respond to a maritime quarantine, Beijing might hope to get away with such a large-scale coercion campaign without inviting serious pushback.

Taiwan’s growing strategic importance makes Beijing’s development of new coercive options more concerning. Washington is no longer maintaining a partnership with Taipei because of a historical commitment or, as Beijing would have the world believe, to needle China. The artificial intelligence boom has put Taiwan at the center of the global economy. Taiwan is a critical supplier for the U.S. tech industry, and the United States recognizes that it cannot be a leader in AI without Taiwan.

The scale of the United States’ economic dependence on Taiwan is revealing. Taiwan is the country’s fifth-largest trading partner; a Chinese blockade of the island would imperil more than $250 billion in trade and could shave more than three percent off U.S. GDP in a year, according to a Bloomberg report. As much as 97 percent of the global supply of the high-end logic chips used in smartphones and other advanced electronics are produced or packaged in Taiwan. Losing access to Taiwanese chips could reduce advanced electronics production globally by 60 percent, with factories forced to rely on their chip inventories. The United States’ auto and medical device industries could deplete their inventories in a matter of weeks. The U.S. firms Amazon, Apple, and Nvidia are among the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company’s ten largest customers, which together represent more than $14 trillion in market capitalization. With AI growth buoying the U.S. stock market and the broader economy, a crisis in Taiwan would trigger a crash—potentially one similar in scale to the stock market crash at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The economic effects of a Chinese effort to squeeze Taiwan would not be limited to the United States. The research firm Rhodium Group has conservatively estimated that a yearlong blockade of the island could cost the global economy between $2 trillion and $3 trillion. A full-scale war would be far worse; Bloomberg has estimated that it would cause $10 trillion in economic losses and a global recession. It is therefore increasingly likely that the United States would be forced to act if Taiwan’s supply chains were put in jeopardy. The cost of standing aside would simply be too high.

Yet just when the United States needs to be doing all it can to prevent a crisis, Washington’s support for Taiwan appears to be wobbling. Trump’s musings about Taiwan’s geographical distance from the United States and his use of arms sales as a bargaining chip are the headline examples, but they are not the only indicators of a shaky U.S. commitment. Policy analysts have argued that the United States should change its position to definitively oppose Taiwanese independence or even withdraw U.S. forces from the military bases in Japan and the Philippines that are closest to Taiwan.

Public opinion in the United States is shifting, too. Americans’ feelings toward China have warmed considerably over the past two years, according to a July 2026 Chicago Council on Global Affairs survey. A majority, 57 percent, support friendly cooperation and engagement with China, whereas 40 percent support an active effort to limit the growth of China’s power. The share of Americans who see China’s territorial ambitions as “a critical threat” has decreased by more than ten percentage points since 2022, and those who favor the use of U.S. troops if China invaded Taiwan has fallen from 52 percent to just 38 percent.

In part, the declining support for defending Taiwan reflects Americans’ growing wariness of instability and conflict. A sense that the world was descending into chaos helped fuel Trump’s 2024 campaign; as president, Trump has heightened that sense by taking assertive military action in places such as Iran and Venezuela. Americans are now suffering the economic consequences of nine months of war in the Middle East, further deepening antiwar sentiment, as the midterm election results vividly demonstrate. Candidates for office used to clamor to sound tough on China, but many now blanch at the idea of suggesting that the U.S. military should defend Taiwan against a Chinese invasion, calculating that this is not the time to be seen as a hawk.

Of course, public attitudes can change quickly during a crisis. If China actually committed aggression against Taiwan, Americans could become more supportive of a strong U.S. response. And if the early stages of a conflict saw American casualties or a Chinese attack on U.S. critical infrastructure, the U.S. public could very well rally around the flag and demand a muscular intervention.

For now, however, China may believe that the United States’ will and ability to fight are both diminishing. The war with Iran has substantially reduced U.S. military readiness for a Taiwan contingency. The United States has used up much of its missile defense stock, including roughly two-thirds of its Patriot interceptor inventory, which was already depleted by U.S. aid to Ukraine, and as much as 80 percent of THAAD interceptors against Iranian drones and missiles. Even before the Iran war, analysts had warned that the U.S. military could run out of long-range, precision-guided munitions in a fight over Taiwan; now, the munitions shortfalls have become perilously acute. The war has also drawn military assets away from the Indo-Pacific. In August, Washington moved its last aircraft carrier in Asia, the USS George Washington, out of the region. It has also relocated missile defense systems to the Middle East, including Patriot and THAAD systems that had been deployed in South Korea.

The result is an increased risk of dangerous miscalculation. Should Chinese leaders assess that the United States’ commitment to Taiwan is wavering in both political parties and that the country is ill prepared for a fight, they might conclude that they have an opportunity to pressure Taiwan without inviting an American response. Yet because the United States has a greater interest in Taiwan today than at any point in history, Beijing’s bet could turn out to be wrong. China could announce a maritime quarantine of Taiwan or another coercive measure only to have the United States intervene, potentially prompting a great-power standoff.

Avoiding such a showdown will require American leaders to recommit to deterrence. First, Washington needs to update the way it communicates its positions. In their public remarks, policymakers should clearly state that the U.S. economy’s dependence on Taiwanese exports makes peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait a vital interest of the United States. American political leaders should emphasize to Beijing that the United States has an obligation to prevent a crisis that would tank the U.S. stock market, cut critical supply chains, and fell many American industries.

Clarifying U.S. interests would not impugn 50 years of careful diplomacy with China, nor would it require any change to U.S. policy as established by the Taiwan Relations Act, the Six Assurances, or the series of joint U.S.-Chinese statements, made between 1972 and 1982, known as the Three Communiqués. The updated statements, rather, would convey to Chinese leaders that certain changes to the cross-strait status quo would be unacceptable to the United States, even if Taiwan were to acquiesce to those changes under pressure. Washington would support a peaceful unification, for example, only if the process guaranteed the security of critical supply chains.

Once the United States makes its interests clear, it will also have to back up its statements with a new playbook to deter Chinese actions that fall below the military threshold. Beijing may already be in the early stages of imposing a quarantine on the island. Washington should not tolerate additional measures that interfere with commerce and maritime traffic in and out of Taiwan. To deter China from taking such steps, the next U.S. Congress should use legislation to clarify its wholesale, bipartisan opposition to Chinese blockades, quarantines, and other restrictions. Even if the White House continued to take a softer position, this would send a message to Beijing that other political actors might force the president’s hand. Congress should also press the administration to prepare punitive diplomatic and financial measures for use in the event of an escalating Chinese quarantine of Taiwan. By planning these reprisals well ahead of any coercive action, Washington would signal that a maritime pressure campaign would entail clear costs for Beijing and carry dangerous escalation risks.

The United States should strengthen military deterrence, too. The next Congress must pressure the Trump administration to release the stalled $14 billion package of arms sales to Taiwan, as well as other security assistance the administration is slow-rolling. Congress has a legal obligation to do so under the Taiwan Relations Act. Pausing security aid violates U.S. policy, and allowing the Trump team to make this concession in its likely quixotic pursuit of rapprochement with Xi only weakens Washington’s hand.

Washington does not have to—and shouldn’t—take these steps alone. U.S. allies such as Germany, Japan, and South Korea would suffer nearly as much as the United States if China were to take control of Taiwan’s semiconductor industry. These countries have an interest in working quietly together to deter and develop joint responses to Chinese coercion while also collaborating to diversify their chip supply chains and make them more resilient. In the United States, this work does not have to wait for a new presidential administration. Congress can send delegations and use other diplomatic opportunities to start developing plans with parliamentary counterparts abroad.

As the 2028 U.S. presidential election approaches, moreover, candidates from both parties should speak clearly about the country’s strong economic interests in Taiwan and about their commitment to deterrence. This does not require embracing bellicose positions, but presidential candidates do need to state firmly that any move by Beijing to choke off vital supply chains would harm U.S. interests and demand an American response. Consistent messaging would also signal to China’s leaders that they should not expect a future administration to be bound by Trump’s policy concessions—and signal to allies that come 2029, the United States will again be a reliable partner in standing up to China’s economic aggression.

The United States needs to update its Taiwan policy, but ceding ground as Trump has done only makes the cross-strait balance less stable. Unlike other Cold War–era policies, the importance of preventing Chinese aggression against Taiwan has become more—not less—vital with the passage of time. U.S. interests in Taiwan are plainer and easier to explain than they have ever been. Only by stating those interests clearly and backing up the words with actions can the United States continue to avert a crisis or conflict that would be devastating for all.

How U.S. Concessions Are Quietly Becoming Chinese Influence

American Strategy Shouldn’t Hinge on an Unwinnable War

Washington Cannot Achieve Tech Dominance on Its Own

How America Can Avert an Unnecessary Rivalry

#5848. American veterans targeted by schemes to steal benefits and exploit the sick, disabled: DOJ

Justice Department officials announced charges against 15 defendants in schemes targeting veterans and VA programs, including a fraud case involving an unfinished cancer treatment center in Florida.

FIRST ON FOX — Fraud schemes drained veterans’ disability benefits and left a promised cancer treatment center unfinished before it was demolished, according to the Justice Department.

In launching a nationwide crackdown on abuse of veterans’ programs, the DOJ is levying charges against 15 defendants in schemes involving more than $3.4 million in intended losses, announcement materials obtained first by Fox News Digital detail.

Prosecutors also secured guilty pleas, trial verdicts and sentencings in cases involving more than $19 million in intended losses during the operation, which began Sept. 1, 2026.

DOJ’S ‘OPERATION GHOSTBUSTERS’ TARGETS MASSIVE STUDENT-AID FRAUD SCHEME BUILT ON FAKE ENROLLEES

A Department of Veterans Affairs sign, left, and the unfinished cancer infusion center at Bay Pines VA Medical Center in Florida. The facility was demolished and never rebuilt after a construction project involving a fraudulently obtained contract, according to the Justice Department. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images: DOJ)

The operation marks the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division’s first coordinated nationwide surge focused on VA benefits, bringing together federal prosecutors, the Department of Veterans Affairs and its inspector general.

"For veterans, benefits are not simply government payments," Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald said in a statement. "They are earned benefits -- earned through service, sacrifice, deployments, injuries, time away from loved ones, and a willingness to serve something larger than themselves."

TEXAS CLINIC OWNER CONVICTED IN $26M MILITARY HEALTH FRAUD TIED TO GOLD-PLATED CYBERTRUCK

Asked during Tuesday’s press conference whether uncovering $19 million in fraud represented a meaningful success given the scale of fraud nationwide, McDonald pointed to the veterans whose benefits and care were affected.

"I would ask the question of the veterans who didn't get the care whether the $19 million that was stolen from them, whether it matters to them," McDonald said. "Whether the cancer center that was not built, did it matter to them that they did not have the cancer center that the taxpayer funded to be able to serve our warfighters and to seek to help them in their moment of need?"

In Florida, the government paid approximately $4.8 million toward a veterans’ cancer treatment center that was never completed — and ultimately was demolished without being rebuilt, according to DOJ.

The VA awarded the $8.9 million construction contract for the Cancer Infusion Therapy Center at Bay Pines VA Medical Center through a program reserved for businesses owned by service-disabled veterans.

Evidence at trial showed that Matthew West, Kevin Kutina and their co-conspirators secured the contract while concealing arrangements under which ineligible companies would perform most of the work and receive most of the payments.

West and Kutina were convicted of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud and major fraud against the United States. Two co-defendants pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

Construction failures plagued the project, leaving the partially completed facility to be torn down, according to the DOJ.

Other cases involved alleged theft directly from veterans’ benefit payments.

To protect your hard-earned VA benefits, stay alert and verify messages through official channels. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

In Texas, prosecutors allege that VA National Call Center employee Heidi Brady used her access to veterans’ personal information and knowledge of payment procedures to change their direct deposit details shortly before monthly disability payments were issued.

The money allegedly went to an account she controlled.

Her neighbor, Raymond Audie Davis, is accused of helping by impersonating veterans during calls to the VA and using their identifying information to redirect payments, according to the indictment.

In Ohio, Darlene Toman allegedly stole from disabled veterans whose finances she was entrusted to manage — including a Marine severely wounded in Iraq who received the Purple Heart and Combat Action Ribbon.

Prosecutors say the victims included people with traumatic brain injuries, schizophrenia, amputations and other serious conditions. Some required around-the-clock care.

Scammers are claiming veterans were overpaid on their benefits by impersonating VA employees. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Rather than safeguard their benefits, Toman allegedly used fraudulent checks and diverted payments intended to cover veterans’ living expenses and care for her own use.

The allegations against Brady, Davis and Toman have not been proven in court. Defendants are presumed innocent unless and until convicted.

Alongside the VA enforcement announcement, DOJ is establishing a Texas Federal Fraud Task Force comprising all four U.S. attorney’s offices in the state, with support from federal, state and local law enforcement.

Fox News Digital's Stephen Sorace contributed to this report.

#5847. Xi Makes the Most of Trump’s Asia-Pacific Trip

World Brief: Xi Makes the Most of Trump’s Asia-Pacific Trip
